speechtext: A message from His Excellency the Governor General transmitting supplementary estimates "E" for the financial year ending March 31, 1964, was presented by Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance) and read by Mr. Speaker to the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The practice of submitting final supplementary estimates at the end of each fiscal year is traditional. These final supplementary estimates E for 1963-64, amounting to $240,884,747 in budgetary expenditures and $56,980,601 in loans, investments and advances, contain the usual miscellaneous adjustments of previous estimates for the current year and certain more substantial items which it has become customary to include in final supplementaries.
As usual, the losses experienced in operations under the Agricultural Commodities Stabilization Act, the Agricultural Products Board Act, the fishermen's indemnity plans and by Canadian National Railways are reported in these supplementary estimates. Farm Credit Corporation and prairie farm emergency fund losses are new items of this sort in these supplementary estimates.
Attention is drawn to three items in the final supplementary estimates for 1963-64. The first is agricultural vote 172e entitled "Estimated amount required to recoup the agricultural commodities stabilization account to cover the net operating loss of the agricultural stabilization board, including loss resulting from revaluation of inventory as at March 31, 1964". The sum of $122.2 million is requested for this purpose. Had this item been calculated on the same basis as in previous years, only $73.8 million would be requested. The additional $48.4 million shown for this item represents the loss inherent in the present inventory of butter solids, butter oil and pork had it been sold at the market prices prevailing on January 31, 1964. This change of method of calculation of loss is designed to reflect more accurately the current position of the program.
In the budget last June I stated that the government intended to deal with the accumulated actuarial deficiencies in the various superannuation accounts. We now propose
that as a general policy the deficiencies existing prior to the commencement of this current fiscal year shall be written off to net debt, which constitutes in effect an adjustment of prior years' accounts and does not enter into the accounts of the current year. The deficiencies created by general pay increases made this year, which the law requires to be charged to this year's expenditure, will of course be so charged. Deficiencies arising from pay increases this year which are not general in scope and therefore not covered by the existing law will be charged to expenditures over a five year period commencing in the next fiscal year. In future the deficiencies arising from pay increases, whether of a general or cyclical character or otherwise, will be charged against expenditures over a five year period commencing in the year in which the increases are authorized.
In accordance with this policy, vote 68e of these supplementary estimates in finance proposes to delete the existing deferred charge from the accounts of Canada and charge to net debt the unamortized portion of the actuarial deficiency of the Canadian forces superannuation account arising in periods prior to the current fiscal year, which is $524.8 million. It also would authorize the writing off to net debt of a similar deficiency of $6.3 million in the superannuation account of the R.C.M.P.
The actuarial liability of some $76 million, including interest, arising from the general increases in pay and allowances granted members of the armed forces in the current fiscal year, will be charged to expenditure this year in accordance with the terms of the statute.
The quinquennial actuarial report on the public service superannuation account as of December 31, 1962, that is, before the current fiscal year, is now being prepared. When it becomes available in a month or two, authority will be sought from parliament to write off then to net debt the deficiency as estimated in that report. The additional deficiency created by pay increases authorized during this current fiscal year will then be estimated and will be charged over a five year period commencing next year in accordance with the policy I have already outlined. The period of five years has been selected because it is the statutory period between valuations of these accounts.

Supplementary Estimates Tabled
Northern affairs and national resources vote 106e includes provision for dealing with the losses incurred by the Dawson city festival. The larger portion of these losses is represented by bank loans and it is proposed to pay these off in full, including interest. These arrangements were guaranteed by the territorial government with the knowledge and consent of the government of Canada. The accounts of a large number of small creditors, many of whom reside in the Yukon territory, are also to be paid in full. It is proposed that the verified claims of the actual promoters of the festival, for expenditures incurred but not authorized, be settled on a basis roughly equivalent to 50 cents on the dollar.

Mr. Speaker, the statement which the Minister of Finance has just read to us is rather technical in nature, and I am sure it is not desirable that I should comment on it at any length even if I were permitted to do so at this time. The minister sent me a copy of this statement a short time ago, and I appreciate his courtesy. This has given me a chance to glance over the statement as he read it. I might say in parenthesis that in dealing with the estimates the minister tabled the other day I was slightly confused in my mythology. I referred to Atlas as rolling the stone up hill when actually it was Sisyphus. Atlas held up the sky. I can correct that statement this morning by saying that Atlas has let go and the sky has fallen, and unhappily it has fallen on the minister.
The Minister of National Defence has been given a great deal of credit for reductions in expenditures, but actually we find that $76 million, including interest, arising from the general increases in pay and allowances for the armed forces must be added by way of expenditure this year. Altogether we get an increase in the deficit for this year of something around $241 million.
I realize, of course, that there are deficiencies for the agricultural stabilization board, as well as these other boards, but this has been a condition for some time. As the minister has pointed out, if these calculations were on the same basis as heretofore the deficit shown here would be substantially less. I am rather intrigued by the last sentence in this paragraph:
This change of method of calculation of loss is designed to reflect more accurately the current position of the program.
I am sure I do not have to be a cynic in order to say that it is also designed to reflect more comfortably the deficit which the Minister of Finance expects next year. Therefore the difference between the two would not be

as great as it would be if he were following the accounting procedures we have followed heretofore.
I am glad to see that it has been decided to write off the deficiency in respect of the superannuation fund. This has always been a thorny problem. Some of us in the house can remember the days which I am sure the Minister of Finance would like to recall, when there were substantial surpluses in the public accounts. The minister of finance would then transfer that surplus to the deficit in the superannuation account, and this would enable him to say "I cannot reduce taxes because we owe the superannuation account so much." This was a very happy policy in years gone by. Unfortunately the Minister of Finance cannot follow that policy today because we have deficits rather than surpluses. At any rate, the government has now decided upon a new policy in connection with these matters, and I presume it will be followed. I think it is desirable that that be done, although it is going to make a substantial increase in our debt and will involve other changes upon which it is not advisable for me to comment at this time.
The last paragraph of this statement refers to the Dawson city festival. I noticed in this morning's newspaper an article on the front page referring to the success of the dramatic act which accompanied this festival, indicating the success which it has attained elsewhere. If in its wisdom some government had decided to cut itself in on a share of the profits of this play, possibly the deficit would not be as great as it now is. I also noticed a reference in the newspaper item to the fact the minister of northern affairs was going to discuss this matter on his estimates. Certainly this is not the time to do so. I am sure at that time we will have a full discussion of this item, as well as the other changes introduced by the minister this morning.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) stopped his remarks rather suddenly when he was talking about the Dawson city festival, and my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce got up before I had a chance to move that the message from His Excellency, together with the estimates presented this day, be referred to the committee of supply.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian wheat board is announcing today the conclusion of a long term wheat agreement, this time with East Germany. This agreement sets out procedures to facilitiate the sale and purchase of wheat through subsequent individual sales contracts.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, March 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Martin (Essex East):
That the treaty between Canada and the United States of America relating to co-operative development of the water resources of the Columbia river basin, signed at Washington on January 17, 1961, together with the protocol containing modifications and clarifications to the treaty annexed to an exchange of notes between the governments of Canada and the United States signed on January 22, 1964, be referred to the standing committee on external affairs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the close of the sitting last evening I had made reference to a study of the Columbia river treaty arrangements and their effects on the United States which had been commissioned by the state of Washington. This study, which was commissioned by the state conservation department, was carried out by H. Zinder and Associates of Seattle, consulting engineers. Hon. members may have seen

a summary of this report which appeared in the Globe and Mail for Tuesday, February 25, 1964. I should like to quote from that article:
A Washington state study released yesterday questions whether development ot the upper Columbia river under a proposed U.S.-Canadian treaty would be of benefit to the Pacific northwest.
Further along the article states:
The report says alternate projects in the United States would provide almost as much power and flood control as the Canadian development at nearly the same cost.
The article also states:
The report says the treaty system by 1985 would provide 485,000 more kilowatts of prime power than the all U.S. system, would probably not make much difference in northwest transmission costs, but might cause higher unemployment in the United States by precluding construction of U.S. dams.
This study, I submit, indicates first, that the accusations made yesterday by the hon. member for Kootenay West as to the competence of the Canadian professional advisers who assisted this government in negotiating the treaty are completely unfounded. They assisted this government in driving a very good bargain with the Americans. It also affirms that the accusation by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that this treaty is a sell-out, and that by its provisions we are conferring on the Americans benefits which they could not provide for themselves in any other way in the United States, is completely unfounded.
When I first commenced my study in connection with this particular subject last year, there were several objections which from a standpoint of an Ontario member, or any other member from central Canada, seemed to be most important to me personally, and would be also of the greatest importance to hon. members from the rest of Canada outside British Columbia.
First, the arrangements which the then government appeared to be in the process of making-if we can dignify the state of immobility which the treaty had reached last year with the description of "arrangements"- would have provided that Canada, at her own expense, would have to raise and pay the full cost of the dams to be built in Canada. At that time it seemed that not a bad analogy to those proposed arrangements was that they were almost like reparations to be paid, and that Canada would assume the full financial cost for the benefits to be provided to the United States in the way of possibilities for the generation of power, and we would not be able to take advantage of these for many years. I submit that it is from that particular point of view in the status of last year's negotiations that the new agreement, whereby the downstream benefits will be sold for a
Columbia River Treaty period of 30 years, appears to be the most advantageous position for Canada to take.
Under the sale agreement the entire cost of structures to be built in Canada will come from the United States, and will not cost the Canadian taxpayers from the Atlantic to the Pacific a single cent. What is more, it will yield a profit in Canada which will enable Canada to instal a portion of the generating capacity at Mica creek dam.

speechtext: What about the cost of "cheap" power?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF TREATY AND PROTOCOL
speechtext:
As the hon. member knows very well, the financial arrangements in this particular treaty will confer upon Canada possibly the cheapest power that can be made available anywhere in British Columbia and probably anywhere else in Canada.
The second concern which disturbed me last year was the fact that under the treaty the Canadian government and Canada as a whole were, by its provisions, made subject to very serious contingent liabilities which, if the contingencies came about, would have been borne by the credit of this country as a whole. There was a significant advance made by this government in negotiating an agreement with the province of British Columbia whereby all liabilities incumbent upon Canada by the terms of the agreement are assumed by that province, the province which will gain the greatest benefits.
Third, I was very much concerned by certain criticisms of the treaty, such as those of General McNaughton to which I referred last night, which indicated that because of the obscurity of the wording in the treaty, Canada's freedom of action to use or develop the waters would be very much curtailed. I made reference last night to the control of the watershed, and in particular to the difficulties which might have been imposed under the wording of the treaty for controlling the waters for maximum generation in Canada.
I was also very seriously concerned at that time about the provisions of article XIII regarding the future diversion of the Kootenay waters. Therefore I was very pleased to see that in the protocol these objections which concerned me had been so effectively covered by the appropriate paragraphs.
I would further like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that while great benefit is to fall in the province of British Columbia under the terms of this treaty, Canadians generally will benefit. As the hon. member for Coast-Capilano pointed out, Canada's balance of payments position will benefit, and the country as a whole will benefit as a result of the activity which will take place when construction commences.

Columbia River Treaty
I would particularly like to point out to hon. members from Ontario that firms such as John Inglis in Toronto and Canadian West-inghouse in Hamilton will have a first class opportunity of competing for the supply of the very expensive and very complicated machinery required for the various installations which, under the terms now arranged, will be proceeded with much earlier than was previously agreed upon.
In this connection I would like to pay a tribute to the Secretary of State for External Affairs who, like I, is a member from central Canada. I should like to pay tribute to him for the skill which he exhibited in these negotiations, and for the benefit which his efforts will confer not only upon the citizens of British Columbia but upon Canadians generally. I am delighted that he-like myself, a native of the Ottawa valley-has been able to participate in conferring such benefits on the residents of the Columbia and Fraser watershed.
I have not made any reference to the remarks of the official opposition as yet, but I listened with interest to the position taken by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revel-stoke, who spoke during the first day of this debate. I suppose his speech might well be summarized in this question: What is the difference, what has been added that was not here previously? The difference between the arrangements completed by this government and the arrangements as they existed last year under the previous government, is the difference between success and failure, the difference between the successful harnessing of a great resource and last year's failure of negotiations and the bitter acrimony being conducted between the federal government and the government of British Columbia.
The hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke apparently had great belief in the prospect of arriving at some advantageous arrangements for Canada. He may have thought his government could arrive at some such arrangements, but that government's chief negotiator, the former hon. member for Kamloops, who had charge of the negotiations for so many years, apparently had no such optimism. In fact he abandoned his treaty, gave up active legislative responsibilities and went into retirement as leader of the Progressive Conservative party in British Columbia.
The position of the hon. members in the official opposition might best be described as having abandoned their own offspring, an offspring which has now been nourished and reared by this government. Now that it has reached a successful status in life, hon. members opposite are coming back in like free loading relatives trying to take credit for it.

As to the New Democratic party, I think I can summarize my remarks about their position in this way. In the one and a half years I have been in this house they have been calling at frequent intervals for committee hearings on this important question. We are now to have committee hearings. But the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said in his remarks the other night it did not matter what kind of evidence was presented at those hearings; they had made up their minds about this treaty, and it was not going to pass.

I intend to say a few words about the contributions made to this debate by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano and the hon. member for Kootenay East, and to reflect for a moment or two on certain words used by the present Prime

Minister when he was leader of the opposition. What these gentlemen have to say now is a far cry from the position they took when they were in opposition.
The hon. member for Kootenay East made, I think, a naive attempt yesterday to reserve his position, or to find justification for reversing his position on this subject. He tried valiantly but, I think, unsuccessfully. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano found himself in the same position, since he too had taken a very different stand when he was in opposition. I intend to put certain facts on record which will show this to be incontrovertibly the case.
Let me deal first with a more specific matter which has arisen in the course of this debate. Hon. members on the government side, in an attempt to garner all the credit for the treaty which was negotiated among the three governments concerned, have played down, as they did when in opposition-particularly the hon. member for Kootenay East- the part which was taken by the able and excellent civil servants who for many years have participated in these negotiations. I refer to Mr. Patterson of the water resources division of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources; Mr. MacNabb, the chief technical adviser to the Canadian government; Mr. Ritchie, Mr. Robertson and Mr. Olson, to mention only a few. These gentlemen were in fact responsible for concluding these negotiations in the way in which they have been concluded, not the politicians as hon. members opposite are attempting to tell us now. The hon. member for Kootenay East, I was told this morning, spent half the night burning up copies of yesterday's issue of Hansard. While I do not entirely credit the rumour, there would be a good deal of justification for the hon. member taking such a course.

There was Mr. Robertson, deputy minister of northern affairs and national resourses. I question whether he has any training in electrical engineering or hydro development. Then the hon. member went on for half a page to describe the virtues of the team from the United States, the team which was pitted against these dwarfs on the Canadian side. I think he was selling the Canadian civil servants short when he was doing that. He says he
Columbia River Treaty has now seen the light. He says he was misinformed and that is why he took the stand he did, before his party formed the government, of supporting the McNaughton plan. Yet here, in the Lake Windermere Valley Echo of January 17, 1963, is a statement by the hon. member in an address to the Windermere district board of trade in the course of which the hon. member said he had been following the course of the Columbia river negotiations since 1949.
All I can say is that it took the hon. member an awfully long time to see the light. If all the information he amassed in those years between 1949 and 1963 finally brought about his conversion, then I think his studies have been both deep and fruitful. However, I doubt the legitimacy of his conversion. As a matter of fact the matter was raised yesterday by a member of the New Democratic group-in fact, it was the leader of the group, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam who said, as reported in yesterday's Hansard:
He used to be a keen supporter of the McNaughton plan, and tonight he has outlined all the defects of the McNaughton plan. I want to ask him when he observed those defects. Was it when he was made parliamentary secretary?
He was referring, of course, to the hon. member for Kootenay East, who then replied:
Effectively, Mr. Speaker, that could be my answer. But the truth is that I have never said categorically that we must have the McNaughton plan. To do so would have meant political extinction for me in the east Kootenays.
Now, that is a most interesting statement, Mr. Speaker.

Columbia River Treaty The fact of the matter is that the hon. member did support the McNaughton plan. As I have said earlier, this is a poor agreement, a poorer arrangement for Canada than was the old Kaiser deal, the deal that was blocked by the International River Improvements Act. I believe it is wrong. I believe this treaty should be renegotiated.

To return to the hon. member's statement that he had never said categorically that we must have the McNaughton plan, may I express the opinion that the hon. member should exercise a little more care in his choice of words. The article I cited states:
Mr. Byrne said he believes that the McNaughton plan is best for Canada and he reviewed important details of the plan which advocates a dam at Murphy creek above Trail, building of the Mica dam and flooding of the Columbia valley-
Mr. Byrne told the meeting he appreciated the thorough study Dr. Coy has made of the Columbia situation although he could not agree with his opinions-
Captain J. S. Blakely, Radium: "What is the situation at the present time?"

speechtext:
"Exactly the same as when the treaty was signed." (January 17, 1961).
Those were the member's words on January 17, 1963. So when the members on my left charge the hon. member with supporting 
the McNaughton plan, the hon. member cannot be heard now to say that he never said categorically that he would support the McNaughton plan.
This weaving and dodging the hon. members like the hon. member for Kootenay East and the hon. member for Coast-Capilano reminds me of when still at school and my reading of "Alice in Wonderland". I should like to cite a passage which came to me and which is to be found on page 117 of Lewis Carroll's "Through the Looking Glass". In this story a discussion occurred between Humpty Dumpty and Alice, and I think we might cast the hon. member for Kootenay East and the hon. member for Coast-Capilano in the role of Humpty Dumpty and Alice just for the moment to see the applicability of these words:
Humpty Dumpty smiled contemptuously. "Of course you don't-till I tell you. I meant 'there's a nice knock-down argument for you!' "
"But 'glory' doesn't mean 'a nice knock-down argument,"' Alice objected.
"When I use a word," Humpty Dumpty said, in rather a scornful tone, "it means just what I choose it to mean-neither more nor less."
"The question is," said Alice, "whether you can make words mean so many diiferent things."
"The question is," said Humpty Dumpty, "which is to be master-that's all."
Alice was too much puzzled to say anything; so after a minute Humpty Dumpty began again. "They've a temper, some of them-particularly verbs; they're the proudest-adjectives you can do anything with, but not verbs; however, I can manage the whole lot of them! Impenetrability! That's what I say!"
"Would you tell me, please," said Alice, "what that means?"
"Now you talk like a reasonable child," said Humpty Dumpty, looking very much pleased. "I meant by 'impenetrability' that we've had enough of that subject, and it would be just as well if you'd mention what you mean to do next, as I suppose you don't mean to stop here all the rest of your life."
"That's a great deal to make one word mean," Alice said, in a thoughtful tone.
"When I make a word do a lot of work like that," said Humpty Dumpty, "I always pay it extra."
Well, Mr. Speaker, I think that is what these two hon. members have been doing here. They have been using words, not-if I may steal a phrase for a moment from an hon. member opposite which I heard yesterday- like the rolling periods of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but words used in such a fashion that they are twisted and warped out of all recognition. I think too we might describe their words, in a more serious sense, as words which are certainly not said in all sincerity. I think the hon. member for Kootenay East made a valiant effort, but to my mind he did not succeed at all. As a matter of fact, I think the only time the hon. member for Kootenay East opens his mouth is to change feet.

Before I conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should just like to refer to what the hon. member for Coast-Capilano had to say before the change of government. He is reported in Maclean's magazine for November 17, 1962 as taking this position:
Dr. Jack Davis, the Liberal member for Coast-Capilano (North Vancouver) a Rhodes scholar who was the senior economist for the Gordon commission and is now his party's chief spokesman on the Columbia. Davis backs the export of power, but considers the present treaty nothing short of a fiasco, because "it fails to procure any demonstrable advantage for the people of Canada." Davis claims that under its terms treaty power costs to Canada will be five to six times as high as the price paid by the U.S.
That seems to be a little different from the position he takes now, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Those comments, of course, applied to the state of affairs which obtained over a year ago. Does he agree with that?

I will agree that the article was written over a year ago and that those statements were made by the hon. member over a year ago, just as statements were made, I take it, since 1949 by the hon. member for Kootenay East. But I am suggesting to hon. members of this house that the only reason for this remarkable change of heart is that hon. members opposite now form the government. They have now seen the light, and have seen that the treaty which was negotiated by this party when it was in office was a treaty which was beneficial to Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Then why did you not ratify it? Why wait three years?

The hon. member knows that negotiations were going on right up until January 22. Not being privy to the secrets of the Secretary of State for External Affairs I do not know the precise date on which the negotiations were concluded, but I suggest that they were not concluded until after-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They were concluded just about January 18.

Then I do not think I am making an inaccurate statement when I say that the negotiations were continuing under both governments, throughout the overlapping period when the government changed right up until January 18.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Would the hon. member permit a question? Does he not agree that before the treaty was signed in Washington it should have been capable of ratification by this house; that it should have been put to the house for ratification when signed by the
Columbia River Treaty executive? Is it not a fact that the treaty was actually incapable of ratification at the time it was signed?

The hon. member knows the circumstances full well. If he has made the study which he says he has made of this matter since 1949 he should know that negotiations were continuing after the signing of that treaty with regard to the details of the sale of downstream benefits and other matters, which negotiations were finally concluded on January 18 and resulted in the protocol. The treaty which was signed was capable of ratification once these details had been ironed out. They have now been ironed out, and I think it ill behooves hon. members now sitting on the government benches, and is rather ungracious of them, to come along as politicians and steal all the excellent work done by the civil servants who ironed out the details of which I speak.
The treaty negotiations which were led by Hon. Davie Fulton when he was minister of justice, and other members of the cabinet, were negotiations which looked after Canada's interests and sovereignty and were for the benefit of Canada generally. We take the position that it is still our treaty. It is the treaty which was negotiated under the former government and which is going to go to a committee and will eventually be ratified by this parliament. It is also the treaty which hon. members opposite, perhaps unintentionally, are now lauding as a good treaty, yet about which they had such critical remarks to make when they were sitting on this side of the house.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit another question? Would he please indicate what financial arrangements had been completed during the regime of the previous government? Were there financial arrangements for the carrying out of the treaty or were there not? Without them obviously the treaty meant nothing at all.

I do not think the hon. member is making that suggestion seriously at all. The financial arrangements which were worked out eventually were the product of the negotiations which continued throughout the remaining term of the former government and into the term of the government which took office last April. But it was the civil servants and the technical experts who worked the matter out. The hon. member knows that because he purports to be one of those technical experts. It cannot be suggested that the politicians worked out the details of the downstream benefits, the height of the dams, the amount of flood control to be provided, and so on. Even those matters, I understand as a layman, are still sufficiently vague to require

Columbia River Treaty
further negotiations for details to be worked out in the future, over a period of some 80 years perhaps. It seems to me that it lies ill in the mouths of hon. members who now form the government to be attempting to steal all the very fine work that has been done by the civil service.

Mr. Speaker, could 1 ask the hon. member a question? As one who is watching from a distance, I would like to know how this is consistent. A few moments ago the hon. member said "our treaty", referring to the Conservative government, and then he talked about the civil service. I want to know, has the hon. member some advantage over the rest of us, that he can have it both ways?

If the hon. member had been listening carefully he would have noted in the course of my remarks-I should not have said "our treaty"-that I said "this treaty", or words to that effect. If he will examine Hansard tomorrow he will find that I did overrun that phrase with another one. I suggest the hon. member should listen a little more carefully.
He is too far away.

I want to deal for a moment with a specific matter which is of concern to me, and I am sure will be of concern to all members of the house. I refer to the development of the Yukon river and to certain remarks that were made by the Prime Minister when he was the leader of the official opposition. His words are to be found on page 4653 of Hansard for 1961. This has to do, sir, not just with an individualistic about-face, which appears to have happened to hon. members over there. It used to be the policy of the Liberal party that there should be no export of power at all, and I will be referring to this later. A proposal was put to the government at the time Mr. Lesage was minister of northern affairs with regard to Yukon development. A decision was then taken that has set back Pacific northwest development for 15 years. This policy was expounded again by the Prime Minister as recently as May of 1961. It appears that he too has now had a change of heart. He said:
It is true, naturally, that any application for the export of power made by any corporation in any part of Canada would have to be considered.
Then he said:
We have learned in the past, however, that one has to be particularly careful about granting permits for the export of power of any kind, however carefully guarded the provisions might be with respect to recapturability, if I may use that word; because experience in the past has shown that when the time comes when you wish to

get that power back from the United States, obstacles are created which make such a course almost impossible.
Therefore, while it would be natural to consider any application for the export of power from British Columbia or any other province in the future, one would hope there would be no departure by any government in Canada from the policy which has been laid down in the past-[DOT]
That policy I have already referred to.
-and, I think, accepted now by governments representing both parties-
He was referring to the policy which in effect was applied to the application of a company to develop the hydro potential of the Yukon river at that time. The government of the day turned down that application.
Active consideration of a power plant for the Yukon river waters began in 1946-47 when the Aluminum Company of America, Alcoa, placed before Canadian authorities a plan to develop 2 million horsepower by diverting Yukon river waters through Bennet lake to tide water in Taiya inlet. This is on the Alaska Panhandle. This was to be done by means of two tunnels, 19 miles in combined length, through the coast range; the head to be developed on the Canadian side and the power to be generated on the Alaska side in the Panhandle.
The United States opposed this development by private companies and suggested a joint investigation of the plan by Canada and the United States, each country being responsible for surveys in its own territory. Canada also opposed the original Alcoa scheme. Mr. Lesage's remarks are to be found in Hansard of either 1946 or 1947, where he said in effect that this power could not be generated on the American side and had to be saved for future generations of Canadians. The Liberal government of the time took the stand that if there was to be any Yukon river power development involving diversion of Yukon waters, Canada would do it and would stand on its rights under the boundary waters treaty to do so.
The studies I referred to were undertaken by Canada and completed, but apparently little work was done by the United States authorities to supplement information they already had. I think Canada's studies were completed in 1950. While various views have been exchanged by the two countries, no agreement has been reached and Yukon power became a quiet issue until late in 1952. At that time is was suggested by the Canadian authorities that Ventures Limited investigate the possibilities of economic power development wholly in Canada using Yukon waters. I was a little out in my quotation

of Mr. Lesage's remarks. These appear in Hansard for 1952 or 1953, and not 1946 or 1947 as I stated.
Ventures Limited immediately began office and field investigations. These resulted in the Yukon-Atlin-Taku project with its early stages producing nearly a million horsepower for construction in 1954. This promise of low cost power evinced immediate interest by large United States industrial firms, and it appeared that construction of the first stages of the Yukon-Atlin-Taku project might be under way in 1954 with Canadian and United States funds.
This was a completely Canadian plan involving the generation of power near Tulse-quah in northern British Columbia. Alcoa was again interested, but United States authorities again did not favour its participation. Later in that year Reynolds Mining Company showed active interest, and in July its top representatives met with those of Ventures in Victoria, British Columbia, and a well known New York consulting and appraisal firm was present on Reynolds' behalf.
The plans for the initial development of nearly one million horsepower were fully approved and agreement for joint participation in construction was drafted for signature. However, on the day the signatures were to be affixed, the Reynolds Mining Company people received word from the head office to sign nothing and return to Pittsburgh. Later it developed that United States authorities did not wish United States company funds applied to the diversion of Yukon waters.
Again, in the fall of 1954 the consulting firm that had advised Reynolds in Victoria showed their interest and met with Ventures officials in New York. The feasibility and economic promise of the first construction stage were again fully considered and accepted, and preliminary construction plans were discussed. However, some two weeks later the company advised that it would not be able to proceed. Again I suggest it was because of United States authorities' disfavour regarding the application of funds by a United States company for the diversion of Yukon waters.
So on three occasions the United States authorities apparently influenced their firms from assisting in the financing of the Yukon-Atlin-Taku project, presumably because this plan involved the diversion of Yukon waters in Canada. By doing so they set back the industrial development of the whole Pacific northwest of Canada by some 15 years, and that setback would apply also, of course, to the state of Alaska.
The Yukon-Atlin-Taku project could be forestalled permanently if any precedent were
Columbia River Treaty set by the treaty we are now asked to consider, and its protocol. Therefore, I am very happy to note the confirmation and affirmation of the principle that the treaty and the deal on the Columbia will not affect the subsequent diversion of any other rivers in Canada, although a great hullaballoo has been made about that. In effect, the protocol in paragraph 8, subparagraph (f) makes a clear statement that the treaty does not establish any principle or precedent that applies to any waters other than those of the Columbia river basin, and does not modify the application of the boundary waters treaty to such other waters. But in effect, Mr. Speaker, the boundary waters treaty already sets that out quite clearly in article 2. Therefore no protocol is necessary to say that we can divert, because it is quite clear in the treaty itself that Canada has the right to divert.
I would hope that the experts, as I am sure they did, had special regard to the Yukon situation when the protocol was considered. If the Columbia river treaty established any such precedent, of course, or if any concessions were made in regard to the Columbia that might affect by precedent the Yukon river, I suggest that storage on the Yukon would be prejudiced. It is vital in my view that no terms should be in the Columbia river treaty or in the protocol that will prejudice Canada's right to use her own Yukon waters as she sees fit, and I intend to pursue this in some detail in the committee.
Since 1959 there has been little or no work done on the once widely hailed Yukon-Atlin-Taku project. The work was done by a subsidiary of Ventures Quebec Metallurgical Industries and included intensive surveys and power marketing talks with United States interests. Since the merger of Ventures with Falconbridge the Quebec Metallurgical subsidiary has survived as a corporate entity, but the Yukon-Atlin-Taku power scheme has been on the shelf for many years.
It would be to Canada's permanent disadvantage to have the Columbia river treaty alter our existing rights on the Columbia, and by inference on the Yukon, to divert waters. So I am very happy to see that this is not so, and I hope I will be confirmed in this belief when the committee considers the project.
The Yukon-Atlin-Taku scheme called for extensive diversion systems in the Yukon river's feeder lakes and rivers in the Whitehorse area near the Yukon-British Columbia border. Canada has rights under the 1909 boundary waters treaty to divert the Yukon river waters, and the Yukon-Atlin-Taku project was based on this right. Eventually the hydroelectric potential of the Yukon will be harnessed, and it is to be hoped that since the

Columbia River Treaty river rises and is fed mainly by waters stored in Canada, we will be the first to take advantage of the hydroelectric benefits to be derived from the Yukon river potential. The old 1909 boundary waters treaty ensured our rights, and I would hope that those rights would remain intact.
Before I sit down may I say a word about the pending Rampart development scheme that it is proposed to undertake in Alaska. I brought this matter to the attention of the Secretary of State for External Affairs last session, and I do so again because the huge potential of the Yukon river system is now in danger from the point of view of preserving its development for future generations of Canadians. The United States army corps of engineers is now in the process of conducting a survey of the feasibility of a completely Alaskan project known as the Rampart project. The report is anticipated very soon, and it is also anticipated that the United States will act on that report at the earliest possible date. If the Rampart project goes ahead we will then become the upstream party under the boundary waters treaty and we will find our position prejudiced.
Even before the government changed this situation had arisen. I drew it to the attention of the previous government and I also, as I have said, brought it before the house last session. It seems to me that we should be sitting down pretty soon, if we have not done so already, with the government of the United States to discuss the future development of the Yukon; because I submit we do not want to be placed in the position of having to face a crystallized program of the Americans to go ahead with the Rampart project when all the engineering assessments as to feasibility and even plans for preliminary construction have been completed with regard to the Yukon-Atlin-Taku project, a wholly Canadian scheme whereby power would be generated wholly in Canada for the use of Canadians. As I have pointed out, the Americans were also determined to go ahead with this project but because of internal politics the companies withdrew their backing on three different occasions.
If something is not done now to negotiate in a friendly fashion with the United States with regard to the Rampart project, I am afraid we are going to find ourselves in the position where we will simply have to junk any hope of going ahead with the development of the Yukon river and its huge potential of some 6 million horsepower in all, I believe. We will have to sacrifice that project because of our failure to react to the

United States plan to develop the Rampart scheme in Alaska.
The Rampart scheme was a secondary alternative that was first proposed, I believe, by Senator Bartlett because of the failure of the Tyee scheme and the Yukon-Atlin-Taku scheme. I understand it is not as feasible from an engineering point of view to develop power at Rampart in Alaska as it is in either of the other two cases. I understand that from an engineering point of view the Tyee scheme was the most practical; and while the power would have been developed on the American side the company, Alcoa, was prepared at that time to meet by long distance transmission all of Canada's demands with respect to any power generated on the Panhandle. That was made quite clear at the time, and for the life of me I still cannot understand the position that was taken by the government of that day in refusing the go-ahead for that project. Here was a wholly American investment of $3 billion to develop some 6 million horsepower, the full potential of the Yukon river and its watershed, with an absolute undertaking on the part of the Americans to transmit all the power required to meet Canadian demands initially and in the future.
Now that the Columbia river treaty is so close to its culmination and ratification I hope the minister will devote his time to sitting down with the Americans and attempting to preserve for Canada a feasible scheme for the development of the whole of the Yukon potential for Canadians.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Spadina.

May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
At one o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 2.30 p.m.

The Columbia river treaty, Mr. Speaker, after long years of preparation was finally signed at Washington on January 17, 1961 by the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, then prime minister of Canada; the Hon. E. Davie Fulton, the then minister of justice, and the Hon. A. D. P. Heeney, then our ambassador to the United States. I have, as a member of the power committee of our party paid a good deal of attention to this treaty over the past one and a half years. I am of the opinion, and I recognize that it is my opinion, that this is substantially a good treaty. I feel that under the political pressures of the day it might

have been signed too hastily and, as a result, the great work of many people over many years may have been unfairly criticized.
The treaty is an involved and intricate, legal and scientific document. For this reason, I submit, it became an easy mark for all manner of criticisms from various sources. From a lawyer's point of view, I found many of these criticisms to be non-factual and indeed, in a great many cases, unfair. Slanderous attacks have been made upon this country's civil servants and their opposite numbers in the United States by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge).
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I made no slanderous attacks. I simply quoted the opinion of the chief negotiator for the United States concerning the ability of our negotiators.

It is a matter of opinion, and I submit I am entitled to my opinion. Since the hon. member for Kootenay West does not appear to have much faith in our civil servants or crown corporations, I may say it is peculiar to find this critical approach coming from an hon. member who espouses such things as the nationalization of industry and administration by civil servants.
No, not by civil servants, but by crown corporations.

Then, we heard a speech from the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas). I understand that this morning he denied a charge by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald) to the effect he had committed his party to blockade this treaty. In so far as this point is concerned, I should like to read into the record from Hansard for March 3, 1964, page 500, the remarks of the hon. member:
If the committee brings back this treaty and recommends its ratification, we in ttie New Democratic party will oppose its ratification, and will do everything in our power to prevent this parliament giving its assent to what we consider a great betrayal of the interests of the people in British Columbia in particular, and the people of Canada in general.
I do not. know whether the leader of the New Democratic party is getting old and just cannot remember what he said three days ago, or just does not want to remember what he said. However, the fact is he committed his party three days ago, to blockading this treaty, but apparently he has changed his mind today.
It is fortunate that there were criticisms of this treaty because some of them, I think all members of the house will agree, were valid. It is fortunate also that the coming into effect of the treaty was made conditional 20220-41
Columbia River Treaty upon ratification by Ottawa. This fact was either known to the signatories at the time they signed the treaty, and they relied upon it, or else it was a very fortunate oversight. We can kill this treaty simply by refusing to ratify it. This would be an unfriendly act. toward a friendly nation. In addition, it would mean the continued wastage of water power for many more years.
What about their 40 years delay on the St. Lawrence seaway?

This would be particularly true in view of the tremendous developments on the Peace river. The co-operative development by Canada and the United States of the water resources of the Columbia will be a source of great strength to both our nations. Apparently the communist party of Canada is convinced of this as well, because it opposes the treaty. I should like to read a couple of paragraphs from a press release dated June 26, 1963-
Was McNaughton a communist?
-which I have received from the headquarters of the communist party of Canada, situated at 24 Cecil street in my riding of Spadina. However, this is a fact of which I am not entirely proud.
The old McCarthy technique.

It is headed, "Communist party of Canada, press release, June 26, 1963-24 Cecil street, Toronto," and reads:

Ratification of the draft Columbia river treaty, as proposed by the Pearson administration and endorsed by B.C.'s Socred government, would constitute a calculated and treacherous betrayal.
-and note the word "betrayal" coming in here again-
-of the vital interests of every Canadian.
Would you read their endorsement of the Canada pension plan?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You are opposing it now, are you?
These words are peculiarly reminiscent of somewhat similar words which we have heard in this house during the last couple of days.
This is nothing but a smear technique. I insist that those words be taken back. That is a cheap smear.

I stand by everything I said, Mr. Speaker. I am convinced that the over-all average of only 2.46-

Columbia River Treaty
Are we going to have the McCarthy technique used in this house?

Order please. The words which were used were not applied to any particular person or party. They were general comment, although I would like to say that the debate at the moment is to refer the treaty to a committee, and is not a general discussion. On the other hand I believe that the scope of discussion was considerably enlarged by several members who spoke before the present hon. member. Therefore, in the circumstances I am relying on the good humour of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge).

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The over-all average of only 2.464 persons per square mile in both the east and west Kootenay areas will rapidly rise, as will the standard of living in the whole area when the dams envisaged by the treaty are built.
Does the hon. member know those comprise one of the highest salaried groups in Canada?

I am very pleased to know that, and I am sure they will do better in future when these dams are built.
The upper Columbia basin in Canada, that is the part north of the states of Idaho, Washington, and possibly a bit of Montana, contains about 40,000 square miles. It is a highly elevated area and its prime wealth is its water. The valley floor in the riding of the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne)-or if you wish, the floor of the Rocky mountain trench where both the Columbia and Kootenay rise quite close to each other-is almost 3,000 feet above sea level.
Have you ever been there?
You betcha.
In an aircraft?

Many times, on foot and otherwise. But Banff on the Bow river, on the east side of the Rockies, is about 4,500 feet above sea level.
I think many people are under the impression that the valley floor of the Rocky mountain trench around Golden, in fact right down to the border, is higher than the land at Banff on the Bow river, on the east side of the Rockies. Such is not the case. Banff is approximately 1,500 feet higher than Golden, therefore a diversion here would be difficult. Even though the Rocky mountain trench will not be flooded under the amended treaty it should still be possible to make diversions to the prairies, particularly later on during the life of the amended treaty.

The proposed diversion from Spillimacheen to the Bow river, that is, from the Rocky mountain trench through a tunnel into the Bow river, is presently estimated to cost $255 million, which is almost the cost of constructing all three dams under the terms of the treaty. A tunnel would have to be drilled through the Rocky mountains for about 25 miles, through which water would have to be pumped up 2,000 feet and dropped into the Bow river above Banff. This tunnel would go through much soft sedimentary rock. Such a tunnel, and others like it that have been suggested would likely give rise to continuous cave-in problems, and would not be too reliable.
The trouble is that Canada is not now ready to proceed with such a venture, or ventures, even if British Columbia would permit them, and that is extremely doubtful. It may be years before such a project could be undertaken. In the meantime the United States, by its increased user, is daily increasing its claim upon the flood waters of the Columbia in Canada. If we fail to ratify the treaty, then they will likely decide to build great reservoirs on the arid Columbia plateau in the United States, immediately south of the border, to trap flood waters coming across the border, to give them the protection they need to settle people on the flood plains further on towards the mouth of the Columbia.
I know there are many difficulties to face in a matter of this kind, and that the negotiations are not always easy because there are so many jurisdictions involved. In Canada the federal government has jurisdiction under the International Rivers Improvement Act, the National Energy Board Act, and by virtue of its responsibility for the conduct of external affairs.
The province of British Columbia, on the other hand, is the owner of the resource, and has primary responsibility for deciding what projects will be built where and when. They say when the dams are to be built and they say where their land can be flooded. We cannot do much about that. In the United States the federal government has more direct control, and it is not so likely to be hamstrung in the course of negotiations by one of its states.
Some will regret that the premier of British Columbia, in the midst of international negotiations over adoption of the McNaughton plan, made it known that he would not allow any flooding of the east Kootenay valley. I am personally of the opinion that the general's plan, for a number of technical and topographical reasons, does get somewhat more power out of the waters of the Kootenay and the upper Columbia; but I am also of the opinion that the premier

of British Columbia had many other things to bear in mind than just a degree of power potential when he made his decision that it would be only the Arrow lakes valley that could be flooded.
In today's world power from coal, oil, gas and uranium are competitive, or are rapidly becoming competitive with hydro power. British Columbia, with the development of the Peace river project, will be glutted with hydro power, and with the proposed developments in Quebec that province will also be glutted. I understand that the present power surplus in British Columbia is in the order of one third to one quarter, and will so continue according to the dominion bureau of statistics five year forecast. So, the brown-out scare, brought up by the 'hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. Fleming), has no basis whatever in fact.
We are not. yet ready to use this tremendous surplus of hydro power, and it seems to me it makes sense to sell it while there is still an opportunity to do so. The downstream benefits from this treaty are not just surplus power; they are a windfall from a waterfall and we owe our deep thanks to General McNaughton. The treaty and the protocol clearly show that in progression, 20, 60 and 80 years after ratification, sufficient water can be diverted from the Kootenay to the upper Columbia so that only the lesser of either 1,000 cubic feet per second or the natural flow will cross the United States boundary in the bed of the Kootenay river. So that easterners may be able to make a comparison, let me say that this border flow cut down by diversions will amount to about one half of the mean flow of the Severn river into Georgian bay, though the Kootenay is a far swifter river and carries much more water.
It seems to me that the general's plan could still be carried out in the future if it were thought feasible to do so. Certainly, the specific diversions could be made for hydro purposes, as they could also be made to the prairies for consumptive use. I think, too, that a good case could be made out for developing hydro with respect to a prairie diversion provided the hydro development was incidental to consumptive use, that is, that consumptive use was the primary purpose of the diversion. In any event, the hydro restriction or limitation can clearly be removed by Canada in 60 years plus a day from ratification by simply serving a ten year notice of termination as provided for in the treaty.
I direct the attention of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to that specific provision.
What has worried me, and I am sure it has worried others, is the possibility that upon
Columbia River Treaty ratification the Americans will immediately take it they have acquired a vested interest in the upper Columbia, an interest which we shall not be able to dislodge whatever our rights may be-that they will build a complex downstream based upon water for the infinite future, not just upon the 60 year period of the treaty. This notion of vesting could arise whether the McNaughton plan or the treaty plan were used, or even if we did nothing at all and allowed the waters to run wild in the untamed river. The way to disabuse this notion, if Canada sees fit, would be to serve the 10 year notice of termination after the dams are all constructed. Canada would have nothing to lose by such a course. We could always at a later date renew the treaty in whole or in part, depending upon whether or not our experience was a happy-one, and in accordance with our needs.
I fully expect that our experience will be-a happy one. The United States has gone a long way to meet our objections by agreeing to the revisions to the treaty as set out in the protocol. One now has to consider first, the benefits of the treaty as amended; second, what better deal could possibly be agreed upon by all concerned; and next the unfriendly situation that would develop if we were to refuse to ratify the amended treaty now.
Like many other hon. members, I was at first sceptical about this treaty, mainly on account of the bad press it had received, but the more I look into it, particularly in view of the improvements and clarifications in the protocol and the sale of downstream benefits, the more I find myself becoming quite enthusiastic about it. I hope to be a member of the committee on external affairs to examine this treaty even further and to question and hear witnesses. I believe the public will be greatly reassured about the treaty after the makers of it have had a chance to present their case before the committee. After all, they have not had an opportunity to do so as yet. Up to this point what we have heard is a lot of one-sided argument.
In the short and long range views, Canada will benefit from the employment that will be provided, tremendous stimulation in the construction industry and related trades, and by a large temporary assist to its balance of payments problem with the United States. British Columbia, after the first 30 years, will have the dams all paid for and will commence to receive power, or firm cash equivalent for its share of the downstream benefits. In addition, British Columbia will receive a great assist towards putting generators on Mica dam that will produce 1,800,000 kilowatts or so of extremely cheap power for a British Columbia east-west grid that can

Columbia River Treaty
become part of a Canadian grid. With the construction by British Columbia of more dams on the Columbia in Canada, I believe something in the order of another 2,200,000 kilowatts can be generated. British Columbia as well as the United States will have their flooding problems alleviated, and there will be over 200,000 kilowatts of found power from the west Kootenay power plants if Libby dam is constructed in the United States, as described by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne).
All in all it looks as if British Columbia is in for a great boom as a result of this treaty, and what helps British Columbia so much is bound to help all Canada. I would recommend that all hon. members make a point of reading the editorial in today's Globe and Mail which appears on page six and is headed: "On with the Columbia Project". It begins with these apt lines:
Great projects seldom would be translated from dreams to realities if those responsible for undertaking them waited until the last objection of the last dissenter had been met.
We now know the general picture. It is a favourable one. So let us really all get down to the detailed facts and learn as much as we possibly can about this unique and promising treaty by sending it to committee.

My remarks will be brief. As one of the members from British Columbia I feel I should put a few facts on the record and raise a few questions with regard to this Columbia proposal. The first point I want to make is with regard to the sale of our share of the power. I know there is a lot of confusion in the minds of some people with respect to the sale of our power and the treaty itself. The treaty in itself is not the instrument for the sale of the power; the treaty merely makes it possible to sell our share of the power. Article VIII of the treaty provides that the Canadian share of the downstream benefits can be sold; the instrument whereby they are sold would be an exchange of notes between the governments of Canada and the United States. So I am referring to the question of the sale of the power separate and apart from the treaty itself.
When the treaty was negotiated by the former government, and up to the time of the signing of the treaty, it was never contemplated by either the Canadian government or the government of the province of British Columbia that any major part of our share of the power would be sold for a long time. That point never arose and was never contemplated. In fairness to the present government I must say that they were forced to consider the sale of the major part or the whole of our share of the power, owing to
tMr. Ryan.]
the position taken by British Columbia in its development of the Peace river. In developing the Peace it became obvious that, if not all, at least a large part of our share of the power would become surplus, and the question of sale therefore arose.
The question I want to ask is this. I am not opposing the sale of power, but is the government satisfied, and will the committee satisfy us, that all of our share of the power will be surplus to the requirements of British Columbia and Canada? When I say "surplus" naturally we must also consider the price. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) made very clear in his speech that he thought the power was generated in the United States and that therefore the question of export did not arise. To me that is a technicality, and is a stand taken by the present government to get out of the difficult position of having to conform with the National Energy Board Act. Surely the government must recognize that the intent of the National Energy Board Act was to have some over-all control of the sale of our energy, and it must certainly be agreed and acknowledged that although the power is physically generated in the United States the causative resource comes from Canada. Even if the government believes that it is not necessary to get a licence for export from the national energy board, why did they not in any case refer this matter to that body, so that we could have some clear evidence that the power which is to be sold at a price is surplus to our requirements? Is the price we are getting right? Can it be substantiated that it is a proper price which we should accept?
I do not say that it is not, but some of the points raised by other members on the other side of the house raise doubt. Using some figures quoted by hon. members opposite I should like to demonstrate that this question is still unanswered. As reported at page 476 of Hansard, the Secretary of State for External Affairs indicated that the price for our share of the power being bandied around varied from 3.75 mills to 5.3 mills. I will use the upper figure which he has quoted of 5.3 mills per kilowatt hour. The Secretary of State for External Affairs went on to explain that included in the 5.3 mills is money which we get for flood control, some $69.6 million which represents .91 mills.
Now, Mr. Speaker, remember this. If our share of the power had been returned to Canada we would have been paid that $69.6 million in any event. Therefore, I do not think it is right to include payment for flood benefits by the United States as part of the sale price of the power, because we would have received that sum in any event if the

power was returned to us. Therefore, using the upper figures of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and deducting therefrom .91 mills for flood control, the price we would come up with, according to the figures of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, would be 4.39 mills per kilowatt hour.
Is this the right price? According to the Financial Post article of June 29, 1963, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) made a statement as follows:
Laing told FP the 3.75 mills price now being bandied about Is merely a breakeven rate. He said Canada would need seven or eight mills if the B.C. government's latest estimates of construction costs were correct.
I am using, as I say, figures quoted by members on the other side of the house.
Then the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Davis) in an article in the Vancouver Sun of February 28, in talking about the price and so on, said:
That is to sell most, or all, of Canada's downstream power entitlement to the United States for cash at a price of, say, five mills per kilowatt hour.
So he says five mills. Therefore, using the figures of hon. members on the other side, the question as to whether the price we are receiving is right or not is left up in the air. I suggest that if the minister, in closing the debate, cannot clarify this point we should at least be given evidence before the committee that the price is right and that the power is surplus to Canada's requirements.
I should now like to make passing reference to the effect of the 11 per cent sales tax on the cost of construction of the dams. The Secretary of State for External Affairs indicated that the price of the dams can be estimated at $448 million (Canadian) in 1973. I think it is obvious to all that any saving in the cost of the building of the dams will reduce the cost of the power which British Columbia will get from the Mica. The secretary of state indicated that there would be $53 million left which could be used to reduce the cost of the power which British Columbia would get from the Mica. Assuming that about half of the cost of the dam would account for materials and equipment, which would be taxable at 11 per cent, the cost of the dams would be increased by roughly $25 million. The secretary of state indicated that the $53 million reduces the cost of the power from the Mica and provides a saving to the people of British Columbia of $16 million per year for 30 years. On that same basis the 11 per cent sales tax on materials increases the cost of the power to the people of British Columbia by approximately $7 million per year, and over 30 years would total $210 million. Later on I will suggest to the government how they
Columbia River Treaty might use the sales tax to the advantage of the people of British Columbia.
The next point I want to make is to set the record straight on the change of position of the present Liberal government from the position taken by the Liberal party in former days. When I heard the Secretary of State for External Affairs speak on Tuesday in that inimitable way of his, particularly in his new political, non-partisan role, I thought to myself that if I could be assured that he would have made such a speech, particularly the remarks he made in the first part of it, I would have invited him to speak on my behalf in the 1961 by-election, aside from the 1962 and 1963 elections.
