speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit me to observe that that would be asking too much of me.

It was just a thought, Mr. Speaker. Then when I heard the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) speak on Tuesday last, his speech sounded like an echo of what the Liberals said in 1961, 1962 and 1963.
I saw the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Groos) here a moment ago, but he is not here at the moment.
I am here.

The hon. member is in the wrong seat. I remember that the hon. member for Victoria opposed me in 1961 and 1962-in 1961 in a by-election and in 1962 in a general election. Then, of course, he saw the light and went across the boundary. In the by-election of 1961 and the general election of 1962 this question was one of the major issues in British Columbia and I was defending myself against attack from all sides. The Liberals and N.D.P.'ers were all attacking me and hammering at me on this question.
And the Socreds.

Yes, and the Socreds. The Socreds changed their minds after the treaty was signed. In any case, Mr. Speaker, this is the position. The hon. member for Okana-gan-Revelstoke (Mr. Fleming) and the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) mentioned some specific facts with regard to statements made previously by hon. members on the other side of the chamber. The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald) had the audacity to suggest that we are now jumping on the band wagon to get some credit. At least one hon. member from that side of the chamber, the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne), was frank enough to come out and say he made a mistake. He said, as is reported at page 608 of yesterday's Hansard,

Columbia River Treaty when he was questioned about his change of position, "I was wallowing in ignorance". That is referring to the position he took before this government assumed office. I had hoped that the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) would show a little contrition also. He may still do so; I know he is a very honest man.
However, Mr. Speaker, if the Liberal party had not taken the stand of opposing us on the treaty question in 1960 and 1962, the results in British Columbia might have been different. This was one of the major issues. Yet today the same people are telling us that this is a wonderful treaty.
Like the nuclear arms question.

Yes. I could talk about that too, but that is a different matter. I suggest that the government should be as frank as was the hon. member for Kootenay East and admit that they made a mistake. There is no harm in that and, as the hon. member said, it is a statesmanlike attitude to adopt. If they do not take this approach, they either do not mean what they are saying, or in 1961, 1962 and 1963 they were deliberately deceiving the people. It is one or the other.
The hon. member for Coast-Capilano says, "Oh, but this is a new treaty. The protocol is a renegotiation". However, we must bear in mind what the hon. member said as reported in the Vancouver Sun of February 28:
The present Columbia river treaty is not good enough. It amounts to a sell-out of our Canadian resources.
This embarrassing treaty must therefore be renegotiated-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member please give the date of that article.
It is February 28, 1963- just before the election in 1963.
Oh, oh.
Does the hon. member for Coast-Capilano dare to say that the protocol constitutes a renegotiation of the treaty?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: An improvement.

If that is the stand they take, I would refute that position with statements made by hon. members on that side of the chamber. In the first place, Mr. Speaker, I would read an excerpt from the joint communique issued on May 11, 1963 by the office *of the Prime Minister and the office of the White House press secretary following meetings between President John F. Kennedy and Prime Minister Lester B. Pearson:
The Prime Minister indicated that if certain clarifications and adjustments in arrangements proposed earlier could be agreed on, to be included in a protocol to the treaty,-

He calls them "clarifications and adjustments". Again, I quote from the second joint statement issued by Prime Minister Pearson and President Johnson regarding the Columbia river development on January 22, 1964. Paragraph 7 says:
The primary purpose of the first set of documents-
That is the protocol:
-signed today was to agree now on the clarifications and adjustments that would eliminate certain possible sources of controversy between the two countries in later years.
That was the official statement of our Prime Minister and the President of the United States. Then in an article in the Financial Post of June 29, 1963, the previous part of the article relating to the difficult position of the Liberals in British Columbia because the federal Liberal government were changing their position, we see the following:
The general Impression is that the changes he has agreed to let Prime Minister Pearson-
This is referring to Mr. Bennett:
-seek in the treaty are only minor ones, and this in turn suggests that the provincial Liberals have forsaken their long standing and outspoken desire for major renegotiation.
If this protocol constitutes a renegotiation, surely hon. members opposite must admit that the major part of this whole question is the treaty. If the protocol constitutes a renegotiation or a substantial change in the treaty, surely the United States congress would have been asked to ratify it. As it is, this is not being done. So the protocol constitutes nothing but amendments and clarifications. The last point I wish to make, Mr. Speaker, is merely to add my support to the appeal made by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke and the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Willoughby) with regard to the over-all development of the Columbia area. I realize that this is primarily a responsibility of the provincial government because it is their resource. However, I take this opportunity to appeal to the people of British Columbia to use their influence with the provincial government. The suggestion is that the government of British Columbia is establishing a Columbia authority, something in the nature of the Tennessee valley authority, to consider a long term plan for the over-all development of the Columbia region.
I	come back to my suggestion to the federal government with regard to the 11 per cent sales tax, which adds roughly $25 million to the cost of the dams.
My suggestion is that the federal government exempt this particular project from the
II	per cent sales tax. I believe this could be done without any amendment to existing

legislation, because the money that is being used comes from the federal government; it is our money. Certainly it is paid by the United States government to the Canadian government, but the Canadian government pays it to the provincial government. Therefore it is federal government money; or at least we can say it is, for the purposes of the 11 per cent sales tax. The exemption from sales tax of the Columbia development could be a lever used by the federal government in getting the provincial government to undertake certain developments in connection with the storages apart from those connected with power. This would have a great deal of value. I refer particularly to the clearing of the shores. I understand that the provincial government has in mind perhaps clearing only the shores of the Arrow lakes. I believe it would be a very shortsighted policy if they did not clear the shores of all the lakes because, as happened in the case of the Tennessee valley authority, the development of the other resources in connection with this project may in time become more important to British Columbia than the power itself. The tendency of the present government of British Columbia in the past has been to be shortsighted in this respect. As far as I know they are not going to clear, for instance, the shores of the lake to be created by the Peace river development. I know from personal experience that it costs much more to remove stumps after they have been in the water for some time. I know of one case where stumps had been in the water for 50 years and they were just as good as when the trees were cut. Therefore my suggestion is that the federal government should in the first place use its influence with the provincial government and that it might use an 11 per cent exemption as a lever to obtain this type of development.
I hope the treaty will be ratified soon. The resource belongs to the people of the province of British Columbia. In the last provincial election this project was a major issue. The people of British Columbia spoke clearly. I think it is now up to the federal parliament to ratify the treaty as soon as possible so that this tremendous development in British Columbia can proceed.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make only a few remarks in connection with the Columbia river project because I do not think any good purpose would be served by my entering into a lengthy discussion of all the pros and cons in connection with this matter-or perhaps I should say reiterating them, because we have heard a good many of the arguments in the last two or three days.
Columbia River Treaty
I was exposed for a longer period and more intensively, I think, to the problems and ramifications of the Columbia river project than anyone else in the house, except the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton). As a result of scores and scores of protracted meetings on this matter it was borne in on me more and more what an extremely complex and difficult question the whole matter was, and how difficult it was to come to a decision with regard to what course of action was the best for Canada as a whole and the best for the province of British Columbia.
In listening to this debate and in paying some attention to what has been said not only by members of the house but by many people outside the house in different places, I have often wished they could have had the same experience I did of listening to such masses of expert advice, engineering detail and things of that kind. Had that been the case I think there would have been far fewer categorical statements made such as some members of the house now wish could be forgotten. Somebody has said that it is much easier to talk about something you know nothing about than it is to talk about something about which you have a great deal of knowledge, and I think many of the statements made about the Columbia river project exemplify that old aphorism very well indeed.
I think there is no question that we could have secured a better treaty with the United States than the one now under consideration. It will immediately be asked: Why did we not get a better treaty? I myself was convinced that a general plan of development very much along the lines of the proposal put forward by General McNaughton would have resulted in greater long term advantages to Canada than any of the other plans which were proposed at one time or another, and there were quite a few of them. However, to adopt what is generally referred to as the McNaughton plan would have involved the flooding of the east Kootenay region, the valley of the Kootenay and the valley of the Columbia running up to Windermere valley. The province of British Columbia absolutely refused to agree to any scheme which would involve the flooding of those areas. This was the basic reason why the McNaughton plan, about which we have heard so much, was not proceeded with.
When we were faced with a situation where the premier and the government of British Columbia absolutely refused to agree to any plan of development which would involve flooding in the Windermere and other valleys as envisaged under the McNaughton plan, we had to search for the next best thing and as

Columbia River Treaty a result the plan embodied in the present treaty was evolved. As I say, I quite freely admit that in my opinion it is not the best plan, but it was the best plan that we could get under the circumstances. It was the best plan that we could get the government of British Columbia to agree to, and I think everyone must realize there was no use trying to go ahead with a plan to which the government of British Columbia would not agree. Therefore the responsibility for the fact that we are now debating a treaty which is not the best treaty that could have been secured must fall squarely on the shoulders of the government of British Columbia. I think there is no question that we did the very best we could under those circumstances.
Instead of spending a great deal of time now dealing with what the advantages of the McNaughton plan were, I think we would be much better off to address ourselves to the realities of the situation and deal with the only plan on which it was possible to get agreement. As I have indicated earlier, this whole matter is so complex in nature that it is not possible to bring out all of the factors involved here in the House of Commons. For that reason I am extremely glad that the whole question is being referred to the external affairs committee. I hope that committee will take sufficient time to bring out all of the factors which were involved when decisions were being made in connection with what plan to adopt and the reasons why various things which might have been desirable were not done and could not be done because agreement could not be reached on them. Unless this is done and until the full story in connection with this whole matter is told, I think there is bound to be a great deal of confusion in the minds of a great many people in Canada and particularly in the minds of many people in British Columbia, which is most directly concerned. Therefore I urge most strongly that there be no attempt to try to hurry this matter through the external affairs committee, but rather that all the time required should be taken there so that the whole picture can be brought out, so that opportunity for full discussion of the whole matter can be provided and all of the expert testimony which is necessary to establish what the facts were can be brought forward and put before the members of that committee.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to enter into this debate but I was provoked to do so by the remarks of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Ryan). I do not propose to follow the hon. member in his quotation of the views 
of the communist party on the issue before us. I had thought that as the communist party has no representation in the house we could be spared hearing what their views were. Indeed, I wondered why the hon. member introduced this subject. I am quite sure it could not have been because he desired to smear all those who in perfect good faith see some weaknesses in the proposed treaty and who desire to examine it accordingly before they agree to its being ratified.
The real reason I wished to intervene was the comment made by the hon. member for Spadina to the effect that opposition to the treaty could be regarded as being unfriendly to the United States of America. I totally deny that proposition, Mr. Speaker. I have too much respect for the United States of America, its government and its people to believe for one moment that, should this sovereign parliament regard the treaty as not being in the interests of Canada and exercise its entitlement, indeed, its obligation to reject it, we need fear that the United States will regard this as an unfriendly act. The reason that the treaty is submitted to parliament for ratification is so that the representatives of the people in parliament can decide whether or not the treaty is adequate for Canada. It was negotiated, no doubt in good faith, by men of very great skill. It has been questioned, also in equally good faith, by able men of high skill who doubt whether or not it is advantageous to Canada.
While I admire the debating ability of my legal colleagues from Toronto on the other side of the house, Mr. Speaker, I suggest to them that before they give their views on this matter they might be well advised to hear the evidence. I anticipate that I may be a member of the committee on external affairs. I do not claim to be completely ignorant of this subject, but I do claim to have an open mind. I hope when this matter is referred to the committee I will listen as carefully as I can to the evidence and try to make up my mind what I believe will be in the best interests of Canada as a whole. I will do this after I have listened to what qualified people have to say, and I doubt very much if lawyers from Toronto are the best qualified experts on this subject.
I noticed that the last speaker, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) suggested that even if this were not the best treaty available for Canada-and he said in his opinion it was not-it would have to be accepted as a result of the veto of the premier of British Columbia. I should like to conclude by saying that if that is so, if the reason for accepting the second best is the premier's veto, then I hope even at this late date it might not be impossible for us

to consider whether we can get a treaty which is in the best interests of the people of Canada, notwithstanding any veto from the premier of one of our provinces.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.

Has
he ever had any direct, personal dealings with the premier of British Columbia?
The answer is no, I have not.

I have been following the speeches very carefully, and I believe there are probably three points in connection with this treaty and protocol which the house and members of the committee should consider carefully. I do not believe these points have been brought out as carefully as they should have been.
The first point is that we are now in the age of nuclear energy. A great deal of time has been spent by all members in considering the power aspects of this treaty and protocol. Having done some research in connection with the development of electrical power from nuclear energy, I find that Canada has taken the lead in this field. The cost of electrical power developed in this way is now somewhere in the vicinity of 3.7 mills per kilowatt. I understand that the 800 megawatt station which was recently constructed on the west coast will result in the reduction of this cost to 2.5 mills. We are considering a treaty which it is expected will result in supplying electrical power 10 or 15 years from now. In the light of the technical advances that are likely to be made in that period, I wonder whether by the time the dams are constructed and power is available we will have progressed so far in the production of electricity from nuclear energy that this scheme will no longer have the value it has now. This is one aspect of the matter which I feel the house and the committee should consider. The power that will be produced under this treaty may not be of the same importance in 1973 or 1975 that it is today.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) referred to another point. This is something about which I agree with him in part and in part I do not. He said that fresh water would be given away, and that this fresh water belongs to the people of British Columbia. He intimated that what we have really done is to sell the water to the arid areas of the United States at a very low price. In other words, the inference seems to be that we should have held up the United States for a greater price. I wish 20220-42
Columbia River Treaty these words could be struck out of Hansard because I, for one, cannot believe that if our neighbour to the south lacked fresh water we would hold up that neighbour for the last penny. I should like to feel that, so long as we are not using the water we would say our neighbour could have it, especially if it will make his fields bloom. I would even like to think that if water became in short supply in Canada as well as the United States we would still be willing to share what we have with our neighbour. The United States has been a good neighbour; no one can deny that. I do not feel that because we have water we should charge a good price. I do not believe this policy has ever been successful in history and I do not believe it ever will be.
There is one final thought I should like to leave with the members of the house and those who will be members of the committee, and it is this: After all, we are dealing with a neighbour, so it is quite possible that our i's have not been dotted or our t's crossed in this treaty and protocol. However, it is our neighbour with whom we are dealing, a neighbour with whom we have had considerable experience. I do not believe these things should be of such serious consequence. I hope that this treaty and protocol will be given a quick passage through the committee and brought back to this house for ratification.

All the
people of Canada, Mr. Speaker, have been very interested in the negotiations that have taken place between one of our western provinces and the federal government, as well as the negotiations that have taken place between Canada and the United States. I suggest that a great deal of confusion has been created, and we have added to the confusion by some of the terms we are using. We now hear reference to a protocol and a treaty. This protocol appears to be to be the political rape of an innocent and misguided nation, accomplished with the co-operation and diplomatic finesse of the establishment.
Would it not be simple for the Canadian people to be told what this scheme really means to Canada? I think everyone who has spoken has made reference to the terms and the arrangements, what we are getting, what British Columbia is getting, what British Columbia will not accept and what the United States wants. This has been done in terms that are not generally understood by the Canadian people. I believe this fact is illustrated by an article in the Seattle Times of January 20, in which this statement appears:
The belief exists south of the 49th parallel that the Canadian public may be in for an emotional let down when the final terms of the Columbia river treaty are announced.

Columbia River Treaty
They go on to explain why. I think the let down is going to take place because the Canadian people will realize we are now playing that little game we always play-let us get rid of our resources if we have nothing we can use them for at present. The previous speaker made this point that, since we are not using this resource ourselves let us give it to someone else.
Have we not been doing this for many, many years? We have resources in this nation that the Americans would be very happy to have. Those who claim to represent British Columbia so well must be aware of the fact that the Americans would be just as happy to get our trees cut up in log lengths, and sent down river to the United States, as they would be to receive the timber material on flat cars after it has been made up into plywood.
I am quite sure there are many entrepreneurs on the west coast who would like that to happen with our other resources as well, but I ask is it not time to look at the implications this will have, and plan for the future? This means looking at the terms of the treaty, and surely the committee to which it is sent will pay the courtesy to the Canadian public of asking whether it meets the needs of the Canadian public, and of asking whether it does anything with the resources of Canada that will help the future of our nation?
The committee must also ask whether this is an arrangement designed to help the premier of British Columbia to raise enough money to build other dams? Certainly this is not a contribution to which we object, but in my opinion it again indicates the inability of the Canadian nation to raise the money necessary to do the developments that we have to undertake.
Let us take a look at some other things that are very similar to this. One is the Saskatchewan river dam project. It was kicked around for 40 years until the Canadian public finally decided that, politically, it was necessary to undertake the expenditure; but that was at a time when the great need for it had disappeared, and when the emergency which gave rise to the project was no longer apparent. If we could have devised a way by which the United States might have financed it, I am certain it would have been built many years before the project was actually begun.
Is it not true we now realize that the amount of water we have been able to provide through that project is not sufficient to meet the needs of the economy of three of our major provinces? Is it not also true that waters from the watershed now under discussion could, in future years, be required for

an irrigation system that will have to be provided in the prairie provinces?
I am not suggesting that this can be done.
I am not suggesting that we want to do it. In fact I am not suggesting that we may ever want to do it; but it is of prime importance to the Canadian nation that we assess the future needs that may develop in Canada, and make sure we do not give away the birthright we have by giving away any more of our natural resources.
I do not know whether the federal government would be willing to advance to the premier of British Columbia the amount of money necessary to develop the electric potential which that premier wants to see developed. I do not know if we could raise that much money, but I do think we had better look at the resources we have and assess whether it would be worth while for us to try to raise that money.
I have no objection to the United States getting the benefit of any surplus resource we have, but I think they should get it only so long as we do not need it in Canada. We in Canada have been fortunate enough to get a small amount of industrial development, mainly because transportation costs were so high that it was easier to transport the financial capital into the country to process our resources here than it was to ship our natural raw resources out of the country.
Water is a very important resource, and in the near future we shall be faced with a decision about the Grand canal. We shall be asked to divert water from the Arctic watershed into the great lakes system where it can be used to promote the industrial development now contemplated in the United States. This is a question which the committee should examine, and it should inquire into who will finance the Grand canal. Are we going to supply the money, or are we going to give the resource to Chicago because they have the financial means to develop it?
If the United States wants power from the surplus production of Canada then we should supply it to them at an economic price, but we should also maintain control of it, both for the present and for the future. This is something which has always been wrong with our nation, and is something we have never been able to solve. We have never been able to match our natural resources to the industrial and economic development that is required, and this is something which should be considered in the committee.
Frankly, I do not give a damn if we ever sign the Columbia river treaty or not. I could not care less. I think this matter is not of

any importance at all, but I certainly do believe we should have the machinery in Canada to assess this resource and find out whether or not this treaty is in our interests. We shall have to set up that machinery, and I serve notice that I shall fight for it.
The "Engineering and Contract Record" points out some of the facts that we will have to consider. In the issue of September, 1962 it said:
So we do not need to rush into any deal we are not satisfied with.
It went on:
It is also said that for Canada to reject the treaty would be a sign of weakness and that we would have to go back to the U.S. and beg for another deal which would give us less than we have now. I disagree.
The reason the bill is submitted to parliament for ratification is so that the representatives of the people can decide whether the treaty is adequate for Canada. It was negotiated in good faith by highly skilled men, but the people still must decide. If parliament does not have the right to reject the treaty, then the process of ratification is a mockery.
If parliament decides that the treaty is not what the country wants, and rejects it, our negotiators can go to the Americans with complete honour and honesty, and say the treaty is not acceptable to the Canadian people. Then both negotiating teams would be obliged to come up with a treaty that is acceptable, and this would mean a better not a worse deal for Canada.
Can the United States afford to make any more concessions and still retain a deal that is acceptable to them? There is no question but that they can. Fortune magazine calls the present treaty a bar-httoiowr 1th' Y'S- because it spends $418 million by 1970 to get extra power that it would have to pay $710 million to obtain without Canada's help.
These figures have been modified, but not changed considerably. In the interests of Canada the committee must look at what the treaty means in terms of the resources of our nation. I am sure members of the press gallery were interested, last night, to hear a man who has criticized the treaty with great vigour and energy while in opposition, suddenly commending it with equal vigour as a supporter of the government. The inference to be drawn is that whether the treaty is a good one or not depends to a large extent upon where one happens to be sitting in the house.
My own view is that the overriding consideration in approaching this question should be the best use of our resources, in the long term, for the benefit not of one province only, but of all Canada. We should take into account the desire we have for a national power grid to supply energy from coast to coast for the secondary industrial development which Canada needs and which is beginning to take place in many areas. I know the minister responsible for piloting this treaty through the house will give some consideration to this approach. I hope he will give the house an 20220-421
Columbia River Treaty indication that the question of making the best use of these resources for the Canadian nation as a whole will be dealt with by the committee before the actual terms of the agreement can be discussed.
It seems to me that even the newspapers have got bogged down in detail. There is a saying in northern Ontario: "You can't see the forest for the trees". It seems to me this situation has been created on purpose in this particular case. I hope the minister will indicate that the over-all care of our natural resources is to become the prime driving force, and that the terms of the treaty will be presented in the light of what they may mean to Canada's future.
Mi. Bert Leboe (Cariboo): I shall not detain the house very long, but there are some things which have been said this afternoon that cannot be left unanswered. It was our intention that only one member of this group should speak on this subject this afternoon because we felt it should go to the committee for consideration as soon as possible. However, I must make some reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) and others about the premier of British Columbia. I should like to make it clear here and now that decisions are not made by the premier of the province, or, indeed, by the premier of any province.
Oh.

Also, as was ably pointed out by one hon. member, there was an election in British Columbia in which the people also spoke in this connection. I resent its being said that the premier of British Columbia has done or said something, as though no reference had been made on his part to the people of that province or to his colleagues.
References have been made to natural resources. I can understand the feelings of my hon. friend, the last speaker, on this question of natural resources because it seems to me that in eastern Canada in the past they have not looked after these natural resources. However, I may say that in western Canada that is not true, and this goes for Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. These provinces of western Canada do look after their natural resources. They do a mighty fine job, and one of the things that is the responsibility of provincial governments is the care of these natural resources on behalf of the people they represent. If anyone says that the provinces should be overridden by the voice of Ottawa in connection with natural resources, he is certainly off on the wrong foot as far as I am concerned.
It has also been said here that the Columbia river treaty was designed to help develop the Peace river. This is absolutely erroneous.

Columbia River Treaty What did happen was this: the Peace river development was the cause of the anxiety about the Columbia project which has been in the news for the last 15 or 20 years. With the alternative power coming out of the Peace it became important, in the opinion of a good many people, to put the Columbia project on the drawing boards and develop it as soon as possible. Had it not been for the development of the Peace river we should not have the Columbia project before us for discussion today. This is all to the good.
Another thing which has been brought up in this debate has to do with financing and the mill rate. When you look at profits from the point of view of cost-benefit ratio and you have to borrow the money to build the complex known as the Columbia river project, you will be faced by having to build your dams in such a way as to get the quickest return from the money spent. Under the present treaty, provision is made for money to come in in a lump sum, and an entirely different situation exists; we are in a position to take advantage of every move we can make to bring about the development at the lowest possible cost. This is bound to have a great effect on our plans for the development of the Columbia river complex. I saw an article in the newspaper the other day in which it was stated that the development proposed at Hamilton falls was only a borderline project at the present time because of the development of power from thermal sources. So the future of this Hamilton project is actually in jeopardy. This means that if any developments are to take place in the use of water power they must take place now. Looking at the cost of the power that comes out of these proposals as compared with the cost of power from developments in the past, it seems to me that the constant dollar ratio must come into play if we are to establish an exact relationship between the cost in the past and the cost at the present time. When we talk about a two mill power rate years ago and compare it with a two mill rate today we must realize there is a vast difference on the basis of the change in the purchasing power of the dollar. I maintain that if we can get power on the line now at two mills or two and a half mills, and hold it there, we shall be getting what amounts to a continual advantage in power costs, bearing in mind the diminishing purchasing power of the dollar.
As I said before, I had not intended to speak in this debate at all. I think we have been confronted with a great many red herrings in the course of this discussion. It is really too bad it has happened, because we could have finished this debate and got the treaty before the committee where we could call on the people we want to talk to, get their

answers and then find ourselves in a position to return to the house and make an intelligent assessment of the subject before us.

So
that Toronto expertise may not be the only voice heard from the east in this debate, I should like to make a very brief contribution. I want to suggest to the house that the Columbia is not the only international river in Canada. I support the treaty and I welcome the protocol, and I have long wondered what all the. fuss is about. I have never understood the reason for a ban on the export of power. I feel that export of power is much like many of our other exports, and that this feature of the treaty is very helpful.
I want to confine myself, not to the technicalities of the treaty, because they will be dealt with thoroughly by the committee, but to certain phrases which have been bandied about lately to which I take objection, such as "losing our sovereignty", "selling our birthright", "sharp Yankee traders", and other colourful yet quite inaccurate statements. As a matter of fact, if we did not have a date to this debate we might think it was taking place in 1864 instead of 1964, and it is really quite ironic that the hon. members who are using these ancient shibboleths are the so-called New Democratic party members.
I admire the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas). We all, of course, admire the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). However, I cannot help saying that they seemed to me to be going through the motions of being horrified and scandalized by certain aspects of the treaty, although they have not yet convinced me that they believe what they say.
I am not in the habit of going through the motions.

I will not make the comment that I could on that. It seems to me that they bow to the altar of the doctrinaire dogma without really getting down on their knees. We must keep this fact in mind, that the Columbia is a supranational phenomenon, not a national one. Surely it should not be so unusual that in 1964 North America should work out a plan for joint development of an international water system. Loose talk about sovereignty is really for the jingoists of other days.
They give them away, no matter what they are worth.

I thank the hon. member for his help; we hear him much easier late on a Friday afternoon.

The hon. member starts his criticism of the treaty from a different set of assumptions than do I. He talks about naivety. Perhaps I am naive, but my assumptions are based on the premise that we are dealing with a friendly neighbour. I am perfectly prepared to believe, and I do believe, that our negotiators are not naive and inexperienced. After all, we have been at this now for five or six years, and that fact itself is evidence of some experience.
I also suggest that we in New Brunswick have had the closest possible relationship with the state of Maine. The national energy board has been authorizing power export for some years. The final protocol, the white paper coloured light green, and the treaty do not affect future developments. In other words, there is no precedent created. In fact, I think I should read into the record the exact terminology. Paragraph 12 of the protocol reads as follows:
Canada and the United States of America are in agreement that the treaty does not establish any general principle or precedent applicable to waters other than those of the Columbia river basin and does not detract from the application of the boundary waters treaty, 1909, to other waters.
In addition to that we in New Brunswick would like to think that the basis for negotiation, the basis for settlement if you like, will work to the advantage of New Brunswick, and therefore to the advantage of Canada in the future development of the Saint John river basin. The headwaters of the Saint John river pass through the state of Maine, and we hope for the eventual development of the Rankin rapids which will assist us in the power developments of the lower stages of the Saint John river in the province of New Brunswick.
Lastly I should like to refer to expropriation and acquisition of land. I thought Dr. Keenleyside's very helpful summary of the Columbia river agreement presented to the Vancouver board of trade on February 10 put the case very well. I have been interested in the St. Lawrence expropriations and in particular the Camp Gagetown expropriations. After all, British Columbia will be making the acquisitions, and I think we must remember that it is not only the owner of the freehold who is affected, but also the people on the fringe of any development. This is one of the great weaknesses in the Camp Gagetown situation and in the St. Lawrence seaway developments, because too many people were adversely affected in a manner which could be measured by standards. That is, you could measure their financial loss, but because they did not actually lose a chunk of land, whether it be one inch of a square mile, did not receive any recompense or compensation.
Columbia River Treaty
I hope that when this matter comes before the committee this point will be brought very forcibly to the attention of the hydro authority of British Columbia or the government of the province, and I should like to think that an entirely new philosophy on land acquisition will be developed in the spirit of Dr. Keenleyside's pronouncements in the last few paragraphs of his speech to the Vancouver board of trade.
That is all I want to say, Mr. Speaker, about this question. I did think that we should remember that there are other places in Canada apart from the Columbia which are affected by this formula, but this great development will be of benefit to North America.
I must inform the house that if he speaks now the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) will close the debate.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments to make in connection with this resolution. It seems to me that this debate illustrates one of the problems created when political chickens come home to roost from time to time, and that in the result probably the waters of this particular issue have been as muddied as are the waters of the Columbia during the appropriate time of year. In the first instance, those who have laboured the question of renegotiation of the treaty have suggested at times prior to this debate, perhaps during the course of election campaigns, that what would emerge would be something completely different in shape and quite distinct from what the previous government negotiated in the form of the treaty signed in 1962, I think it was. However, I think they will now be confounded, first by the fact that the hon. gentleman who opened this debate for the government quite frankly admitted that in form the protocol did not, in essence, change in any material way the initial treaty. I think there is a very sound reason for that, apart from anything else, which I do not think has been mentioned so far. The very fact that this is termed a protocol, the very fact that there is not a new treaty, that the old treaty was not renegotiated establishes, I think, that these were conditions essential to the completion of the final arrangements between the United States and this country. I may be wrong in this, but as I appreciate the situation, if there had been a renegotiation which would in the end result have produced something quite different in form than what was in existence before and if there had been a new treaty, the whole matter would have been laid before the senate of the United States. Then a completely fresh approach would have been taken

Columbia River Treaty and there would have been discussion in that legislative body. As I apprehend the situation, it was for this reason that what is added to the treaty is called a protocol, which in international parlance means, I think, something in the form of a supplementing or a qualifying document. This is all it is.
As I said before, I think the hon. gentleman in opening the debate virtually admitted that, and in doing so cut the ground from under the feet of those who at different times in the past have said this was not what was going to be done. They said there would be something new, something fresh; a completely new position and attitude would be adopted by a Liberal government if and when it came into power. Now we find this is included in the protocol by reason of the fact that the treaty could not in essence be changed without being resubmitted to the United States senate. I think this is the answer which must be given to those who took a different position.
I do not want to go too much into past history, Mr. Speaker. This was done in that eloquent and articulate statement by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) earlier in the day. But I do recall-this was at the time in 1961 when the then prime minister first announced to the house that the treaty had been signed-the present Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, took what I think was the sensible and logical approach, namely that the treaty should not be put before the house-by inference I think this meant, of course, that it should not be put before the external affairs committee-until there had been executed and completed an agreement between the government of Canada and the government of British Columbia. This was the position which the government accepted. It attempted to negotiate this agreement and, as was said earlier, the present government carried on and in due course successfully concluded the agreement which is now in the form of the treaty and the protocols.
I submit that this was the sensible attitude to take. But it was not the attitude that was consistently maintained by the Liberal party which now constitutes the government. In 1962-and it is significant that this was very shortly before an election; it was in the dying days of the parliament which was dissolved prior to the election in June of 1962- the leader of the opposition completely reversed his field and said, "Let's put the matter before a committee right now". He was followed by the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), who quoted copiously from statements which had been made by General McNaughton. He quoted them in such a way as to leave no other inference, I think, but that he accepted those

statements. Certainly by quoting them he, as an experienced member of parliament, realized he was accepting their correctness. I am sure he will be met with those statements during the course of the meetings of the external affairs committee and he will probably take an entirely different position at that time. The minister quoted those statements and said, "Let's all together discuss this matter". He was referring to discussing the matter in the external affairs committee. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, this was done because an election was imminent and the hon. gentleman at that time
Who is not a politician anymore.

At that time he was a politician and realized there might be some significance to this particular issue. I think this was unfortunate, because this has been a difficult and complex problem. I for one, living where I do and representing the area which I do, am happy that the matter has been completed. In essence I believe that the treaty as slightly qualified and amended constitutes in its entirety a document which will probably have a beneficial effect, although I say this with the reservation that I would certainly like to hear the evidence given before the external affairs committee with respect to one or two of the issues which have been raised by General McNaughton and others. I am thinking particularly of the statement made by Mr. Ripley which appeared in an egineer-ing magazine two or three years ago.
Robert Ripley?

I do not know if it is Robert Ripley. I do not know the gentleman's first name. Anyway, I refer to the statement he made relating to the question of reversing the flow of the Columbia and the comparative acreages that would be flooded. These are very material points. While I accept in general the principles of this treaty as qualified by the protocol, I do so with that particular reservation.
Mr. Speaker, something has been said about the Peace in relation to the Columbia. It was said they have been tied together, and I do not think there is any doubt that there has been more than causal connection as to effect and the relation between these two great river projects. I have always taken the position that these were both necessary and essential projects for the benefit of our country. I have continuously supported the engineering and the hydroelectric project which the province of British Columbia has commenced and is carrying forward vigorously on the Peace. I had the pleasure of going up into that area in the constituency of my

friend the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe) and seeing the tremendous works which have been undertaken on this particular river. I have every reason to believe that both projects will be required and the electrical energy produced from both will in due course fill a very important requirement in Canada. I think there is a very definite connection here. I raised during the last session the fact that in my view, despite the admission by the then minister of justice that the Peace river was a navigable river, and despite the fact that according to the opinion given to the minister by his officials, it came under the provisions of the Navigable Waters Protection Act and the government of British Columbia was proceeding without obtaining the necessary approval required under that act. In my humble opinion this is entirely linked up and identified with the negotiations which were carried on with regard to the Columbia and was a case of appeasing the province of British Columbia in order to work out a complete, negotiated agreement in respect of the Columbia.
I have to say I am only surmising but I can surmise nothing else in view of the admissions which were made last session by ministers of the crown. If this is so, I think it is a shocking thing. I support in every way the principle of the Peace river dam but I do think it should proceed according to the law of this country.
I have one further comment to make. I wish that it could have been possible for the whole question of waters and rivers to have been considered as one over-all subject and the fact is that some time it will have to be. I was reading the other day that in the United States the greatest amount of water that can ever be available in that country as a result of engineering works will be 650 billion gallons a day and that by the end of this century the population of the United States will be such that their requirements for industrial, consumptive and irrigation purposes will be not less than 1,000 billion gallons a day. In other words, there will be a shortfall of approximately 350 billion gallons a day.
I agree with the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather) that this matter will first of all have to be dealt with on the basis of national development, including such rivers as the Columbia and the Peace and then ultimately on the basis of continental discussion and agreement. The re-use of waters in the east and the proper use and division of the waters of the rivers of the west between industrial purposes, irrigation purposes and consumptive purposes will have to be considered, not by any one province, not by the federal government alone but in my view by
Columbia River Treaty a consortium of the provinces and the federal government. This has proven to be a necessity in the United States.
We hear much talk nowadays of amendments to the constitution. The British North America Act now provides that jurisdiction over navigation is vested in the federal government but I think this will have to be looked at very critically, and changed. For the sake of those who will come not too long after us the only sensible and rational solution will be to take an over-all look at the question of the use of the waters of this continent.

The hon. member for Edmonton West. Before the hon. member speaks may I say I know he will appreciate that we are discussing whether the treaty should be referred to the standing committee on external affairs.

Mr. Speaker, it may have been that Your Honour and I had some system of telepathy working in this regard, because my first remarks were going to be as to the nature of this debate as it has developed since last Tuesday. I trust that in so doing I will not be deemed to be criticizing Your Honour or your deputy, but I think that in all of these matters, where there is a resolution either to set up a committee or to refer something to a committee, there is a rather narrow issue. I do not think we need to go into the precedents in that regard. No doubt Your Honour has had reference to them in the same way that I did.
But I would say that for the Chair to limit the debate becomes very difficult indeed when the minister leading off throws in the whole question at issue; and, as for the fact that the debate has extended as long as it has, I believe that, while the honourable and genial Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) has been extremely patient, he brought the length of the debate upon himself. Last Tuesday we were also subjected to a great trial of our patience as we listened for about two hours to his speech. I think that the lengthy speech made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs must have been motivated by some pride of authorship, because it certainly covered the whole ambit of the Columbia river treaty situation. It certainly did not deal only with the very limited issue of referring the treaty to the committee and the advantages of doing so. We got the whole question from stem to gudgeon.
The hon. gentleman dispensed his favours left, right and centre. He paid tribute to the negotiators and, I thought perhaps a little grudgingly, to the previous administration, in order to make what I felt was quite a

Columbia River Treaty concession on his part-that the treaty was basically a good one and that he felt the protocol improved it. As a matter of fact, the burden of his two hour speech was really to show that the protocol was a great improvement on the treaty. I do not think it went any further than that. As a matter of fact, if one looks at the press release rather carefully he also sees the same type of authorship. It seems that the same people had a hand in the preparation of the press release as in the preparation of the material for the minister to make his speech, not only as to sentences but to whole paragraphs. In any event, the matter has been put on the record in all its details.
Under those circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I think the house must accept a reply in kind. The debate has ranged far and wide, and once the house has embarked on such course I think it must necessarily remain with it until the debate is finished. Otherwise those who follow find themselves rather frustrated by the restrictions. There is always that difficulty, and I think what has happened may be a salutary lesson to those on the government benches, that if any minister introducing a motion of this kind wishes to have a short debate he should limit his remarks and not open the subject matter too widely.
This debate has once more shown the attitude of the Liberal party. In my mind it is a reaffirmation of the remarkable changes in attitude that have come about as the result of the assumption of office. In fact, if one considers similar major matters of government policy, nuclear arms, devaluation, the Canada pension plan as well as the treaty we are now considering, we find that at the time of the election and prior thereto great stands were taken by hon. gentlemen opposite from the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) down but once they assumed office we saw a remarkable volte face. In fact, last night we almost had the situation of one hon. member eating himself because his about face was so dramatic. But he at least had the good grace to admit that he had changed his mind. Why he did so I do not know. I refer, of course, to the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) who, in fact, confessed that if he maintained a certain stand it would be political suicide for him in his constituency. How cynical can he be? Is he there affirming that political expediency shall always prevail, that in order to curry favour with his electors he is going to maintain one stand but in his heart he believes he should take another? I believe this is an attitude on the part of the hon. gentleman that is not to be commended.

In any event, we see this attitude exhibited by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), and it was referred to by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). In the years gone by we have heard him quote remarks passed by this person or that person, including General McNaughton, with the inference that there was something wrong with what had been done, and that there was a great deal of weight in the criticism that we were being offered. Then, in so far as the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) is concerned, I shall refer in greater detail to some of the speeches he made in 1962 about the Columbia river. I find it absolutely astounding that he should stand before us now and make the representations he does in the light of what he said and wrote previously.
We are now told that this was basically a good treaty. It has always been the position of the former administration, that this was basically a good treaty. There were certain difficulties with it, yes. It could not be said that 100 per cent had been gained on every point because, after all, we were negotiating with another country. As was readily admitted, I think, by both the minister and the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister, there is a certain amount of give and take in any negotiations. It seems that when these hon. gentlemen were in opposition they concentrated on the things that were being yielded to the United States. Now, we have seen the protocol which is the result of these renegotiations. I shall refer in a few moments to the words of the hon. member for Coast-Capilano.
In his speech in the house in 1962, as recorded at page 204 of Hansard, we find these words:
As a Canadian I regard this treaty with mixed feelings. As a legal document it is superb. Phrased in straightforward language, it takes a complex subject and reduces it to terms most, if not all, of which are understandable to the layman.
In the light of what has happened in the protocol, these are rather illuminating words:
The engineering data upon which the draft treaty is based is laudable.
We have not heard from the hon. gentleman at this time, perhaps in committee we will, as to why this information was any less laudable or why it should now be acceptable to him if the treaty is still basically a good treaty and is acceptable to him.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Will the hon. member accept a question?
Yes, certainly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Has it not been brought to the hon. member's attention that the cost estimates, for example, have been markedly-altered in recent months?

This is a point upon which I think the hon. member is now getting himself into difficulty. He is emphasizing the inconsistencies in what he said last night, because he referred to the $274 million (Canadian) that we would be getting for the sale of downstream benefits. He said that this would go toward covering the cost of certain installation and would leave us with some $50 million or $60 million which could be applied to the cost of generating electric power. I say to him in that regard not to be naive, because these costs will be going up and up. I say that, rather than having $50 million left over we will be looking for $100 million more. These projects are of such a vast nature, and so complex, that anyone who says they are going to cost so many millions and no more is indulging in a little bit of fantasy.
It is true that there have been changes in the cost estimates. It may be recalled that the treaty was based on negotiations during 1961. We are now in the year 1964, and the renegotiations, or what passed for renegotiations, were in the year 1963 when already there had been changes in costs. I think, perhaps, the example has pointed up the difficulty of fixing a hard and fast limit on the costs of these projects.
If I may, I should like to quote again from page 204, where the hon. member is reported to have said:
New information has been collected since the treaty was negotiated nearly three years ago.
This fact is borne out by the hon. member.
Construction cost estimates have been revised and interest rates have risen sharply. Still, it is the over-all economics of the Columbia river treaty about which I am most concerned. As interpreted publicly by the present government it must be characterized as nothing short of a fiasco.
Is the treaty a fiasco?
It is inconceivable that the government of this country should enter into any agreement, let alone a comprehensive treaty with another country to last at least 50 years, which failed to procure any demonstrable advantage for the people of Canada.
On December 13, 1962, the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) had this to say as recorded on page 2643 of Hansard:
As I have said earlier, this is a poor agreement, a poorer arrangement for Canada than was the old Kaiser deal, the deal that was blocked by the International River Improvements Act. I believe it is wrong. I believe this treaty should be renegotiated. '
The hon. member for Coast-Capilano said much the same sort of thing and he used the
Columbia River Treaty word "renegotiation". What does renegotiation mean? Does it mean merely dotting the i's and crossing the t's, or the clarification of certain language? This is all that the protocol has done, it has clarified certain language. I submit to hon. members, and to members of the government, that it is not within the power of the United States to enter into an agreement or treaty and then negotiate fundamental changes which one would expect from renegotiations. If the treaty was so wrong, as hon. members pretended, then more would be required than the mere negotiation of a protocol which does not have to be submitted to the senate. This must mean that these are essentially minor changes, and in many places the protocol does nothing more than dot the i's and cross the t's. We can always work on improving the language of a treaty or any other document. I cannot see that there has been anything take place that one might classify as renegotiation.
It is true that we now have the sale of surplus power and this was not the case at the time the hon. member was speaking. Certainly, however, this principle had been set out in the speech from the throne, and this had been a change in policy by the government. But it was a policy that had been so instituted and held to so hard by hon. members opposite when they had been in power prior to 1957. The Secretary of State for External Affairs was a member of the administration that refused and said no, no, a thousand times no, to the sale of power outside this country. This is very definitely a fact, and there had to be a change because of the change of circumstances.
I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs will agree that today, because of changing circumstances, we in Canada can consider, under appropriate conditions, the sale of power resources on a long term basis. It does not do us any good for natural gas to be in the ground. It does not do us any good to have hydroelectric potential merely going over some waterfalls or rapids, or running through undeveloped basins. It is only when we harness these resources that they are of advantage to us. But then there is always the technological process which must follow, and right close behind hydro is nuclear power. We must realize that it does not lie too far in the future. It may be a matter of a decade, perhaps two decades-and I may be ultra conservative when I say this-when nuclear power will be a real competitor to hydro generated power. Therefore it behoves us to develop these resources and to realize them. Today we have billions of tons of coal lying underground and they are of no use if they remain there unrealized.

Columbia River Treaty
Therefore we must understand that one of the chief purposes of the negotiators at the time the protocol was being drawn was to sell the downstream benefits rather than to continue with what had originally been decided upon, that electric power to the equivalent of 50 per cent of the downstream benefits would be delivered at a gate in Canada.
We must also realize the difficulties that faced the previous administration over the years, and which I am sure the present ministry came into contact with last summer when they were negotiating with the government of British Columbia. The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe) said this was not the action of the premier of British Columbia, but the premier of British Columbia is the government of British Columbia. These negotiations were carried on by him on behalf of his government, and we know that attitudes in that province have changed considerably.
We also know that the actions of the government of British Columbia have been approved by the people of British Columbia. These are facts of life. We know that there was an about face at the time that General McNaughton was, shall we say, underlining the alternatives of diversion of the Columbia into the Fraser, and we know that the government of British Columbia pulled the rug out from under his feet in this regard and did not leave him with much bargaining power.
We know also that the government of British Columbia was fully represented on the bargaining team dealing with the United States, and at that time the terms were acceptable. I ask you to consider the position when a provincial government sends a cabinet minister as a member of a negotiating team and he approves of what is negotiated. Then nothing is said, but months after that the provincial government suddenly says it does not approve. Whose word can we take? There must be some responsibility. However, this was a fact of life that had to be faced, that after the treaty had been signed with the United States we suddenly discovered that British Columbia did not consider the terms exactly acceptable.
By that time, of course, the Peace river power question had loomed much more largely, and the government of British Columbia saw a way to obtain financing for it. It had previously made sure it was the only customer, through its nationalization of the B.C. Electric. When you are dealing with somebody else and he has certain aces up his sleeve, you have got to be able to cope with the situation.
I am sure the Secretary of State for External Affairs will agree that it has not been easy

dealing with the province of British Columbia, and I am sure that under the circumstances, so far as Canada is concerned, he will now agree this is basically a good treaty. The official opposition agrees with him. I do not think the protocol hurts the status of Canada with regard to the treaty, although I have some reservations regarding the entire sale of the downstream benefits.
I also have some reservations regarding the cost of power that will be generated on the Peace river, and it is possible that at some stage there will be some difficulty in British Columbia. However, this is a decision for the people of British Columbia, and we know that in the last provincial election they gave the government of Premier Bennett another mandate. Therefore his scheme has received a certain stamp of approval. The people of British Columbia are the owners of the resource and, if they have committed a mistake, they will have to bear the brunt of it. It will be regrettable, but that is a decision for them to make, the same way as the original decision on the export of gas was a decision of the Alberta government. Those are political decisions that have to be taken, and of which the people either approve or disapprove.
In reviewing the stand taken by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) I must say I cannot agree with him, but at least he has been honest and consistent in that stand and his opposition to the treaty. I do not think we have seen any vacillation on his part, but I must say there was in many other sectors.
You mean the hon. member for Kootenay West, not Kootenay East.

I beg your pardon. Mr. Speaker, I am having some difficulty and I may have to ask you to rescue me. It was certainly the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) who I said was honest in his stand.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: You were right the first time.

Other Liberal members were converted, especially Liberal members from British Columbia who used to be very critical of this treaty. They paraded up and down, and the whole hierarchy of the Liberal party is responsible for a similar state of affairs. They cannot take any glory out of this, even though in his attitude the other afternoon the Secretary of State for External Affairs seemed to feel that his should be all the glory, and that this beneficence to Canada was brought about as a result of the expert negotiating team which he led.
His biggest problem has been smoothing the Liberals down.

I feel, myself, he will have a great deal more difficulty spreading salve among a lot of Liberals in British Columbia. They are talking out of one side of their mouths one day while they are thinking something entirely different. That is why I find the conduct of the administration in this regard somewhat reprehensible. I wish they had been more honest about their stand in the past.
A great deal has been said in the course of this debate about water wastage in Canada. Perhaps you will allow me a little latitude, Mr. Speaker, to refer to this aspect of the subject. We in Canada do have immense opportunities in this regard. Not only is water needed for industry in western Canada, but water is needed in Ontario for all purposes. As far as we in western Canada are concerned, it is needed for agriculture, and I should, myself, like to see an immediate study made of our water resources and their use across the country. Such a study should be undertaken in co-operation with the provinces. This is not something which should be undertaken only when the urgency becomes extreme; we should do it now, because, after all, we have in this country tremendous rivers which flow to the north. One considers, for example, how much water diversion could take place from the head of the Mackenzie water system, which is the cradle of the Athabasca.
Somebody spoke about the diversion of Peace river water to the prairies. I do not know who is going to build the great canal which would be required; remember, there are large heights of land, acute heights of land, between that river and the prairies. Certainly, though, out of the Athabasca system we could, without too great an expenditure of funds and dislocation of land use, divert sufficient water to help our prairie systems. We should recognize that there must be a degree of co-operation between the provinces; I do not think a province can go it entirely alone as far as the best use and development of water resources is concerned.
I hope this suggestion will commend itself to the heads of the various provincial governments as well as to the federal government-that they should get together and make a comprehensive study with a view to the full development of these water resources.
I feel that we will get a lot of answers- certainly, we will get a lot of questions- during the hearings of the external affairs committee. No doubt there will be differences of opinion. There will be differences of opinion on technical matters and judgement decisions will have to be made. People are not going to be 100 per cent right or 100 per cent wrong, and it is for this reason
Annual Vacations Act
I differ from my genial friend from Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge); I do not think he is entirely right, nor do I believe he is entirely wrong. Those people who also have opinions, or who have written or said things on which the hon. member bases his conclusions may, in the same way, be not wholly right and not wholly wrong. However, we may get some clarification of these various points in the course of the committee hearings.
Essentially, though, there has been no difficulty about referring this question to the committee on external affairs. There has, of course, been a great deal of controversy about the treaty, and I myself would like to see some clarification of a number of points though, in essence, I believe we must go ahead with the scheme. I would, therefore, commend it to hon. members with perhaps some minor alterations, after we have got a little more information.
