Annual Vacations Act
He said: Once upon a time-that, of course, is the way one begins to tell a story about something which took place a long time ago -there was a national convention of the Liberal party in the city of Ottawa.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: PROVISION FOR TWO WEEKS HOLIDAY AFTER ONE YEAR
speechtext: Was that in 1919?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR TWO WEEKS HOLIDAY AFTER ONE YEAR
speechtext: That was in 1919.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TWO WEEKS HOLIDAY AFTER ONE YEAR
speechtext: A good convention.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR TWO WEEKS HOLIDAY AFTER ONE YEAR
speechtext:
I hear hon. members across the way speaking as though they know something about the Liberal convention of 1919. Among other things, it committed the Liberal party to the enactment of the various items of a national labour code. We have reminded the Liberals of this many times and it occurred to me today that they might be getting tired of hearing of this 45-year stint of theirs to try to bring in this national labour code.
I wondered if by any chance they had dealt with this matter at an earlier convention. There is one thing about Liberal conventions; you do not have to go to very many books because they have not had very many. The one in 1919 was called the second convention; the first one was held back in 1893. I went to the library to see whether there was any record, and I found an interesting booklet entitled: "Official report of the Liberal convention held in Ottawa June 20 and 21, 1893". So I thought I would look in this booklet to see whether there had been any suggestion made for the adoption of a national labour code, and do you know, Mr. Speaker, I cannot find the word "labour" in the book. It is not in the index, and I have spent most of the afternoon reading through the book and did not find the word "labour" anywhere. So I will not accuse the Liberals of having proposed a national labour code 71 years ago; it was only 45 years ago that they first made this proposal.
Now at long last, in the year 1964, we have had it promised in the speech from the throne that there will be introduced at this session a national labour code. And not only was it indicated in the speech from the throne, but when he spoke in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) confirmed that that legislation would be introduced. Likewise the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) when he spoke in the same debate confirmed this fact. Therefore we are looking forward to the introduction at this session of this piece of legislation which has been a Liberal promise now for 45 years.
I have taken careful note of the references which have been made to the proposed national labour code, because I have been

hoping that it would be comprehensive in scope. There is always the possibility that it might be, but so far the references made to the items of detail which might be included are not as comprehensive or as extensive as some of us feel they should be. So far the only references have been to a minimum v/age, maximum hours of work and a maximum work week, statutory holidays with pay, and certain other standards which, I take it, are in the field of protection of workers against injury and accident. But to date there has been no clue given on the part of spokesmen of the Liberal government as to whether anything is going to be done to improve the vacations with pay legislation which is already on the statute books. Therefore, I suggest it is a fortunate coincidence that before the introduction of legislation from the government for a national labour code this bill of mine comes up for debate, giving us the opportunity to present to the government the proposal that this year, when we are going to enact a national labour code, we do the job in its entirety.
We feel that the Annual Vacations Act which is already on the statute books should be improved in at least two particulars. As a matter of fact I have on the order paper two bills dealing with the two proposed improvements, one of them being the bill now before the house. This bill simply provides that the two weeks vacation with pay which is now made available to workers who come under federal labour jurisdiction after two years of employment be made available to them after one year of employment. The other suggestion I make, which as I say is in a separate bill so that hon. members are not faced with the problem of having to vote for two things at the same time-because this other suggestion will come later-is that after five years of employment the length of holidays with pay should be increased to three weeks.
In these times, Mr. Speaker, surely proposals such as this-two weeks after one year and three weeks after five years-are minimum standards which our economy ought to be able to provide. At any rate, what is before us at the moment is not the whole broad scope of a national labour code. What is before us at the moment is not the question of three weeks after five years, but simply the question of providing for two weeks vacation with pay after one year. As I say, a vacation with pay is one of the items of a national labour code which is already on the statute books, having been put there in the session of 1957-58 when the Conservatives were in power. At that time we tried to persuade the government of that day that if they

were going to give us an Annual Vacation Act two weeks should have been available after one year. The Liberals supported us then in the contention that the bill should have been improved right at that time. They also supported us later when they were in opposition in 1962-63. So that when one looks at the record of the various groups in this house he finds at some point that all of us have supported the idea that we should be much more generous in our provisions for holidays with pay than we have been to date.
All that the bill now before us proposes, Mr. Speaker, is an amendment to the Annual Vacations Act which is now on the statute books. The act now provides that workers under federal labour jurisdiction do not get their two weeks vacation with pay until they have worked for two years for an employer. This bill would amend that statute so that workers under federal labour jurisdiction would get their two weeks vacation with pay after working one year for an employer. It seems to me that this is a very simple and minimal provision. All of us are in favour of it, and therefore I hope the bill will get the support of the house this afternoon. I hope it gets not only the support which it had last year, namely speeches in favour of it, but the kind of support which the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien) received the other day for his bill, namely its actual passing through all stages of the house.
I have tried to think, without success, of some title to the bill which would be as bilingual as the phrase "Air Canada". If I could have done that I suppose the chances of this bill would have been better; but at any rate, in whatever language it is put, surely we all want to give our workers under federal labour jurisdiction the best we can in terms of annual vacations. We want to give a lead to the country as a whole. Therefore I hope that this afternoon the house will pass this bill.

Since there is no obligation to bring that point into the discussion, it could also bring out financial difficulties with great consequential effects on other points of negotiations which also have their importance.
I understand that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred to the speech from the throne in which the government announced its intention to bring forward legislation to lay the foundation of a labour code and that this item was not specifically mentioned.
However, I think we must rely on a good understanding of the wording, especially when we know that this labour code will deal with the main points concerning labour rights. It is not necessarily restrictive. Of course, vacation is a very important matter; that is a very important fringe benefit, but it was not possible for the government to reveal all the points to be brought forward in the legislation and I think it is an accepted policy that the government always holds back a trump card in case it has to negotiate.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the government will deal with this question when it introduces its labour legislation.
I do not believe that this question of vacation could be defined in terms other than "working standards". I am sure that hon. members realize that the same serious reasons of justice and opportunity that existed in 1958 when that legislation was passed should prevail today.
As the present government is concerned with the welfare of Canadian citizens and their present needs, it is conscious of its responsibilities to the working class and to the employers alike. Based on past experience, it is also thankful for the excellent suggestions made by hon. members.
I am convinced that the government intends to integrate the main acts concerning labour relations, working conditions and other benefits into a single piece of legislation which should be simpler and easier to apply. At least that is what I concluded from a perusal of the speech from the throne.
If today the government decided to pass the bill introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I wonder whether such action would not bring a senseless upheaval of Canadian economy, at least in

Annual Vacations Act
certain fields, because, in two or three months from now, when the government introduces its labour legislation, or rather a rudimentary-labour code, further changes will be called for.
The standards existing when the present legislation was enacted in 1958, are still unchanged. Government statistics reveal that about two thirds of the people employed in industry are only entitled to two weeks paid vacation after having been employed for two full years.
On the other hand, some provinces did not choose to legislate in this matter, and, if I understand rightly, the two most densely populated provinces, that is, Ontario and Quebec, only provide for one week's vacation after two years employment.

This act does not apply to employment under a collective agreement entered into after the coming

This bill, as it stands, would appear to be a simple measure designed to give a new employee two weeks holiday with pay after working for one year. I do not believe it is quite that simple. Immediately, there would have to be changes in contracts, in pay scales and employment time and there would be added expense. Today, Mr. Speaker, added expense is something that is of major concern to me, not only as a member of this house but as an employer and as a Canadian taxpayer. Surely in this country, where today we are devoting 12 per cent of personal incomes, as against 8 per cent in Great Britain and 7 per cent in the United States, to welfare and where our welfare costs have risen from 2.8 per cent to 6 per cent of the gross national product in the last 12 years, we must stop continually looking for new ways to add to the cost of doing business. I would be the last person or almost the last person to deprive a fellow worker of a week's holiday with pay, even though I have never had that luxury.
In the past, I have spoken in favour of a balanced budget, and one way to do that is to reduce costs. I have seen very little of that since I have been here, especially in the last few days. Deficits may be necessary or

justified in certain periods of extreme unemployment and recession. As soon as those conditions are corrected, we should plan for a return to a balanced budget. We have not heard any talk about recession for two or three years, and unemployment is at its lowest level since 1957. We still hear about more and more spending and large deficits. I say the Canadian parliament is so imbued with the give, give philosophy, the continual build-up of government staff and departmental expenditures, that we find it impossible to cut expenditures as we must. If we cannot operate economically and effectively as a government, what hope have we of leading our country's industry to a productivity level to pay for the pleasures and welfare we have already voted ourselves.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) pointed out that we have been discussing this measure for some time, but if it takes another few months to incorporate it into a comprehensive measure to be presented to the house, I am in agreement with the delay. I think the whole bill should be well studied and discussed, so that the end product will be one that will be accepted and applauded by all sides of the house and by industry. Then I am sure industry will decide, if the legislation is good, to use it as a yardstick for their own plans.

I do not want to seem prejudiced even though, as I said, I never enjoyed a holiday with pay. My poor father never believed in holidays, with or without pay. He worked for 18 years, and after five children and a heart attack, he once decided to take a holiday. It was the only one he had, and I remember it well because he came home with a case of acute indigestion. The change was too much for him.
We did not have another holiday until we all came home from the services in 1946, when we once more joined him, and this time it was a holiday with pay from the R.C.A.F.
As I say, I am not prejudiced but I do worry, with the expanding economy and declining unemployment rate we have today.
